label: Design databases
prereqs: Netlists as the shared currency of the flow
The map of design representations and formats
lesson:
# Design databases

A design database is the in-memory model that every engine of a physical design tool reads and edits: placement, routing, timing, extraction and verification all work on the same objects. Older flows passed files between point tools, re-parsing the design at every step. A tool designer cares because the database fixes what each engine can see, how fast it can query, how changes propagate to other engines, and how large a design fits in memory.

## Why tools share one database

When each tool reads files from the previous one, every step pays to tokenize LEF, DEF, Verilog and Liberty, resolve names and build its own model. On a design with 10 million instances, parsing alone can take minutes per step, and each tool's private model can drift from the others. A shared database is built once and then edited in place: the placer moves instances, the resizer swaps masters, the router adds wires, and every later engine sees those edits immediately. The database becomes the single source of truth. That only works if engines edit the shared objects rather than keeping private copies, and if derived results (arrival times, congestion maps) are kept in the engines and refreshed when the design changes. File formats remain, but as interchange at the edges of the flow: reading the inputs, writing the outputs, and handing data to tools outside the database.

## What the database stores and links

A physical design database keeps three kinds of data apart. Technology data comes from technology LEF: layers, directions, pitches, widths, spacing rules, vias and sites. Library data describes master cells: size, pins and their shapes, obstructions. Design data describes this chip: instances, each pointing to its master, with location and orientation; nets; instance terminals joining an instance pin to a net; block ports; rows; and routed wires. The links run both ways. From an instance the tool reaches its terminals and from each terminal its net; from a net it reaches all its terminals and their instances. So the question "which nets touch U17?" is a walk over the four terminals of U17, not a scan of a million nets. Masters are stored once and shared: 40,000 NAND2 instances hold only their placement and a reference, while pin geometry lives once in the master.

## Derived results, change and persistence

Not everything an engine computes belongs in the database. Placement and wires are design data. Arrival times, slacks, congestion per gcell and wirelength gradients are derived: they can be rebuilt from the design, so they live inside the engine that owns them. That split forces a mechanism: when the placer moves 200 cells, the timer's cached arrivals near those cells become stale, so the database must notify interested engines of edits, and they mark the affected results dirty. Persistence is the other half. A binary checkpoint of the object tables reloads far faster than re-parsing DEF and keeps objects and properties that DEF cannot express. Two further design choices recur: references between objects are stable handles, so that a deleted object is detected rather than dereferenced, and names are interned once in a string table so that hot objects stay small.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design: From Graph Partitioning to Timing Closure" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 1; the OpenROAD documentation for OpenDB.

A design database is described as the single source of truth for a flow. What does that require of the engines?

A) They each write their own output format

B) They edit the shared objects instead of keeping private copies

C) They run in separate processes

D) They never modify the design
problems.a: They edit the shared objects instead of keeping private copies
problems.e: If an engine keeps a private copy, the copy and the database drift apart. Engines read and write the shared objects, so a later engine sees every earlier change.

label: Blocks, instances, nets and terminals
lesson:
# Blocks, instances, nets and terminals

Every netlist database names the same handful of objects: a block (the design), instances of master cells, nets, and terminals where nets meet pins. OpenDB calls them dbBlock, dbInst, dbMaster, dbNet, dbITerm, dbMTerm and dbBTerm. Getting the counts and links right is the first step in sizing a database, writing a parser that fills it, and choosing a graph model for an algorithm. This lesson counts terminals, connections and the edges a graph expansion creates.

## Instance terminals and block terminals

A master cell has pins, called master terminals. An instance is one use of a master in the block. Each pairing of an instance with one of its master's pins is an instance terminal (ITerm), the object a net actually connects to. The block's own ports are block terminals (BTerms). So the number of ITerms is the sum over masters of instances times signal pins. Example: 12 NAND2 cells with 3 signal pins, 8 inverters with 2 and 5 flip-flops with 3 give $12 \cdot 3 + 8 \cdot 2 + 5 \cdot 3 = 36 + 16 + 15 = 67$ ITerms. The block's 20 ports are 20 BTerms, a separate object kind with its own geometry on the die boundary. Power pins are often handled separately, as special connections, so state which pins are counted. ITerms usually outnumber instances by a factor of 3 to 4, which makes them the largest object population in the database.

## Nets as hyperedges of terminals

A net is a set of terminals: one driver and one or more sinks, possibly including BTerms. In graph terms the netlist is a hypergraph whose vertices are instances (or terminals) and whose hyperedges are nets. Each connected terminal belongs to exactly one net, so the total number of net-terminal connections equals the connected ITerms plus the BTerms. Example: 800 ITerms, of which 6 are spare outputs left unconnected, plus 24 BTerms give $800 - 6 + 24 = 818$ connections. Spread over 240 nets that is $818 / 240 = 3.41$ terminals per net, the average net degree. Most nets in real designs have two or three terminals; a few clock and reset nets have thousands. Averages hide those high-fanout nets, which dominate the cost of algorithms that are quadratic in net size.

## Expanding nets into graphs

Many algorithms, such as quadratic placement or spectral partitioning, need an ordinary graph rather than a hypergraph. The clique model replaces a net with $p$ terminals by an edge between every pair: $p(p-1)/2$ edges. A star model adds one new vertex per net and connects it to the $p$ terminals: $p$ edges. Example: nets with 2, 4 and 7 terminals give $1 + 6 + 21 = 28$ clique edges against $2 + 4 + 7 = 13$ terminal entries in the hyperedge form. A 1,000-terminal clock net alone would add 499,500 clique edges, which is why tools either use stars for large nets, drop or reweight them, or skip clock nets. The database therefore stores the hyperedge, the compact and exact form, and each engine builds the derived graph model that suits its algorithm.

## Going deeper

The OpenDB documentation and its header files for dbBlock, dbInst, dbNet and dbITerm; Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 2.

problems.q: A block holds 33 instances of DFF_X1 (3 signal pins), 12 instances of AOI21_X1 (4 signal pins) and 36 instances of XOR2_X1 (3 signal pins), and the block itself has 5 ports. In an OpenDB-style object model, every signal pin of every instance is one instance terminal (ITerm) and every block port is one block terminal (BTerm). How many ITerms does the block hold?
problems.e: An ITerm is the pairing of one instance with one master pin, so the count is the sum of instances times pins: 33 x 3 + 12 x 4 + 36 x 3 = 255. The 5 ports are BTerms, a different object kind.

problems.q: A block holds 23 instances of NAND2_X1 (3 signal pins), 29 instances of OAI22_X1 (5 signal pins), 37 instances of NOR2_X1 (3 signal pins) and 24 instances of DFFR_X1 (4 signal pins), and the block itself has 15 ports. In an OpenDB-style object model, every signal pin of every instance is one instance terminal (ITerm) and every block port is one block terminal (BTerm). How many ITerms does the block hold?
problems.e: An ITerm is the pairing of one instance with one master pin, so the count is the sum of instances times pins: 23 x 3 + 29 x 5 + 37 x 3 + 24 x 4 = 421. The 15 ports are BTerms, a different object kind.

problems.q: A block holds 9 instances of AOI21_X1 (4 signal pins), 15 instances of BUF_X2 (2 signal pins), 25 instances of INV_X1 (2 signal pins) and 6 instances of NOR2_X1 (3 signal pins), and the block itself has 18 ports. In an OpenDB-style object model, every signal pin of every instance is one instance terminal (ITerm) and every block port is one block terminal (BTerm). How many ITerms does the block hold?
problems.e: An ITerm is the pairing of one instance with one master pin, so the count is the sum of instances times pins: 9 x 4 + 15 x 2 + 25 x 2 + 6 x 3 = 134. The 18 ports are BTerms, a different object kind.

problems.q: A block has 670 ITerms, of which 0 are left unconnected (spare outputs), 20 BTerms, each on a net, and 219 nets. Every connected terminal sits on exactly one net. What is the average number of terminals per net? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Each connected ITerm and each BTerm contributes one terminal to one net: 670 - 0 + 20 = 690 terminals. Divided over 219 nets that is 3.15 terminals per net, the mean hyperedge size.

problems.q: A block has 430 ITerms, of which 11 are left unconnected (spare outputs), 35 BTerms, each on a net, and 108 nets. Every connected terminal sits on exactly one net. What is the average number of terminals per net? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Each connected ITerm and each BTerm contributes one terminal to one net: 430 - 11 + 35 = 454 terminals. Divided over 108 nets that is 4.2 terminals per net, the mean hyperedge size.

problems.q: A block has 380 ITerms, of which 0 are left unconnected (spare outputs), 33 BTerms, each on a net, and 112 nets. Every connected terminal sits on exactly one net. What is the average number of terminals per net? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Each connected ITerm and each BTerm contributes one terminal to one net: 380 - 0 + 33 = 413 terminals. Divided over 112 nets that is 3.69 terminals per net, the mean hyperedge size.

problems.q: The database stores each net as a hyperedge: one net object with a list of its terminals. An algorithm that needs an ordinary graph expands every net into a clique, one edge per pair of terminals. The nets are n1 with 7 terminals, n2 with 3 terminals, n3 with 9 terminals and n4 with 3 terminals. How many graph edges does the clique expansion create?
problems.e: A net with p terminals becomes p(p-1)/2 edges: 21 + 3 + 36 + 3 = 63 edges, against 22 terminal entries in the hyperedge form. The quadratic growth is why the database keeps the hyperedge and lets each algorithm choose its own model.

problems.q: The database stores each net as a hyperedge: one net object with a list of its terminals. An algorithm that needs an ordinary graph expands every net into a clique, one edge per pair of terminals. The nets are n1 with 9 terminals, n2 with 8 terminals, n3 with 7 terminals and n4 with 6 terminals. How many graph edges does the clique expansion create?
problems.e: A net with p terminals becomes p(p-1)/2 edges: 36 + 28 + 21 + 15 = 100 edges, against 30 terminal entries in the hyperedge form. The quadratic growth is why the database keeps the hyperedge and lets each algorithm choose its own model.

problems.q: The database stores each net as a hyperedge: one net object with a list of its terminals. An algorithm that needs an ordinary graph expands every net into a clique, one edge per pair of terminals. The nets are n1 with 4 terminals, n2 with 2 terminals, n3 with 7 terminals and n4 with 7 terminals. How many graph edges does the clique expansion create?
problems.e: A net with p terminals becomes p(p-1)/2 edges: 6 + 1 + 21 + 21 = 49 edges, against 20 terminal entries in the hyperedge form. The quadratic growth is why the database keeps the hyperedge and lets each algorithm choose its own model.

label: Hierarchy and instancing
prereqs: Pre-order and post-order traversal of a rooted tree
lesson:
# Hierarchy and instancing

Designs are written hierarchically: a top module instantiates cores, which instantiate ALUs, which hold leaf cells. A database can keep that hierarchy, storing each module definition once and referring to it from each instance, or flatten it into one level of leaf cells. The choice decides memory, how edits work and how names are formed. Physical design engines usually work flat, while hierarchical storage pays off for repeated blocks, layout (GDS) and hierarchical verification.

## Flattening a module hierarchy

Flattening replaces every module instance by a copy of its contents, recursively, until only leaf cells remain. Count bottom up. Suppose alu holds 400 leaf cells, core holds 150 leaf cells and 4 alu instances, periph holds 90 leaf cells, and top holds 20 leaf cells, 3 cores and 2 periph instances. One core flattens to $150 + 4 \cdot 400 = 1750$ leaves. Top flattens to $20 + 3 \cdot 1750 + 2 \cdot 90 = 5450$ leaves. This is a post-order traversal of the module tree: each module's flattened count is its own leaves plus the sum of child counts times multiplicities. Flat names concatenate the path, such as core_1/alu_2/U7, so they grow with depth, and a flat database must store every one of those 5450 instances with its own placement.

## Definitions versus occurrences in memory

A hierarchical database stores each definition once: one object for each leaf cell and each child-module instance inside each module. In the example, top has $20 + 3 + 2 = 25$ objects, core $150 + 4 = 154$, alu 400 and periph 90, for 669 objects in all, against 5450 in the flat form, a saving of 4781. The saving grows with replication: a chip with 64 identical cores stores one core definition. Layout formats exploit the same idea; a GDS structure is referenced many times. The price is that per-occurrence data, such as a location, a routed wire or a timing value, cannot live in the shared definition, because each occurrence has its own. Tools that keep hierarchy must keep occurrence data in separate tables keyed by hierarchical path.

## Occurrences and uniquification

An occurrence is one path from the top to an instance of a module. With 3 cores each holding 4 alus there are $3 \cdot 4 = 12$ occurrences of alu, all sharing one definition. If an ECO resizes a cell in core_1/alu_2 only, editing the definition would change all 12. The tool must first uniquify: copy the definition into a new module, say alu_u1, point that one occurrence at the copy and edit it. Synthesis does the same when one instance of a module is optimized differently from the others. Uniquification trades memory for independence, and repeated uniquification drifts toward a flat design. That is one reason physical design engines such as those in OpenROAD operate on a flattened netlist and keep the hierarchy only in names or in optional module objects.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 1; the Yosys manual on the hierarchy and flatten passes.

problems.q: Module top holds 53 leaf cells, 8 instances of module core and 1 instances of module periph. Module core holds 150 leaf cells and 3 instances of module alu. Module alu holds 770 leaf cells. Module periph holds 80 leaf cells. How many leaf-cell instances does the flattened design contain?
problems.e: Flatten bottom up: one core contains 150 + 3 x 770 = 2460 leaves. Top contains 53 + 8 x 2460 + 1 x 80 = 19813 leaves.

problems.q: Module top holds 48 leaf cells, 5 instances of module core and 1 instances of module periph. Module core holds 240 leaf cells and 5 instances of module alu. Module alu holds 570 leaf cells. Module periph holds 220 leaf cells. How many leaf-cell instances does the flattened design contain?
problems.e: Flatten bottom up: one core contains 240 + 5 x 570 = 3090 leaves. Top contains 48 + 5 x 3090 + 1 x 220 = 15718 leaves.

problems.q: Module top holds 21 leaf cells, 7 instances of module core and 2 instances of module periph. Module core holds 390 leaf cells and 2 instances of module alu. Module alu holds 340 leaf cells. Module periph holds 480 leaf cells. How many leaf-cell instances does the flattened design contain?
problems.e: Flatten bottom up: one core contains 390 + 2 x 340 = 1070 leaves. Top contains 21 + 7 x 1070 + 2 x 480 = 8471 leaves.

problems.q: Module top holds 15 leaf cells, 4 instances of module core and 1 instances of module periph. Module core holds 340 leaf cells and 2 instances of module alu. Module alu holds 410 leaf cells. Module periph holds 240 leaf cells. A hierarchical database stores each module definition once: one object per leaf cell or child-module instance inside each definition. A flat database stores one object per flattened leaf cell. How many fewer instance objects does the hierarchical database store?
problems.e: Hierarchical: top 20 + core 342 + alu 410 + periph 240 = 1012 objects. Flat: 4895 leaves. Saving: 4895 - 1012 = 3883.

problems.q: Module top holds 57 leaf cells, 7 instances of module core and 2 instances of module periph. Module core holds 50 leaf cells and 3 instances of module alu. Module alu holds 810 leaf cells. Module periph holds 460 leaf cells. A hierarchical database stores each module definition once: one object per leaf cell or child-module instance inside each definition. A flat database stores one object per flattened leaf cell. How many fewer instance objects does the hierarchical database store?
problems.e: Hierarchical: top 66 + core 53 + alu 810 + periph 460 = 1389 objects. Flat: 18337 leaves. Saving: 18337 - 1389 = 16948.

problems.q: Module top holds 18 leaf cells, 8 instances of module core and 1 instances of module periph. Module core holds 190 leaf cells and 6 instances of module alu. Module alu holds 480 leaf cells. Module periph holds 110 leaf cells. A hierarchical database stores each module definition once: one object per leaf cell or child-module instance inside each definition. A flat database stores one object per flattened leaf cell. How many fewer instance objects does the hierarchical database store?
problems.e: Hierarchical: top 27 + core 196 + alu 480 + periph 110 = 813 objects. Flat: 24688 leaves. Saving: 24688 - 813 = 23875.

problems.q: Module top holds 8 leaf cells, 8 instances of module core and 2 instances of module periph. Module core holds 330 leaf cells and 3 instances of module alu. Module alu holds 510 leaf cells. Module periph holds 120 leaf cells. An ECO must change one particular alu, reached through one particular core. How many distinct occurrences (hierarchical paths from top) of module alu exist, all of which share the one alu definition until the design is uniquified?
problems.e: Each of the 8 core instances holds 3 alu instances, so there are 8 x 3 = 24 occurrences. Editing the shared definition would change all of them, so the tool first uniquifies: it copies the definition for the occurrence being edited.

problems.q: Module top holds 17 leaf cells, 8 instances of module core and 1 instances of module periph. Module core holds 190 leaf cells and 5 instances of module alu. Module alu holds 800 leaf cells. Module periph holds 260 leaf cells. An ECO must change one particular alu, reached through one particular core. How many distinct occurrences (hierarchical paths from top) of module alu exist, all of which share the one alu definition until the design is uniquified?
problems.e: Each of the 8 core instances holds 5 alu instances, so there are 8 x 5 = 40 occurrences. Editing the shared definition would change all of them, so the tool first uniquifies: it copies the definition for the occurrence being edited.

problems.q: Module top holds 7 leaf cells, 3 instances of module core and 2 instances of module periph. Module core holds 220 leaf cells and 2 instances of module alu. Module alu holds 300 leaf cells. Module periph holds 340 leaf cells. An ECO must change one particular alu, reached through one particular core. How many distinct occurrences (hierarchical paths from top) of module alu exist, all of which share the one alu definition until the design is uniquified?
problems.e: Each of the 3 core instances holds 2 alu instances, so there are 3 x 2 = 6 occurrences. Editing the shared definition would change all of them, so the tool first uniquifies: it copies the definition for the occurrence being edited.

label: OpenDB
lesson:
# OpenDB

OpenDB is the design database at the center of OpenROAD. It descends from the Athena database and its schema follows LEF and DEF: technology layers and vias, library masters and pins, and a block of instances, nets, terminals, rows and wires. Every OpenROAD engine, from floorplanning to detailed routing, reads and edits the same OpenDB objects in one process. Knowing its object model is the entry point to reading or extending any OpenROAD tool.

## Technology, libraries and blocks

OpenDB separates data by origin. A dbDatabase holds one dbTech, built from technology LEF, with dbTechLayer objects for each routing and cut layer (direction, pitch, width, spacing) and the via definitions. Library LEF fills dbLib objects holding dbMaster cells, each with dbMTerm pins and their shapes and obstructions, plus sites. The design is a dbChip with a top dbBlock, built from DEF or from a Verilog netlist plus floorplan commands. The block owns dbInst instances, dbNet nets, dbBTerm ports, dbRow rows and the routing. This mirrors LEF and DEF so closely that reading DEF is almost a direct mapping of sections to object creation, and writing DEF back is a traversal. Timing data is not in OpenDB: Liberty is read by OpenSTA, which keeps its own library model and links to OpenDB instances.

## Navigating instances, terminals and nets

The links follow the object model. A dbInst points to its dbMaster and owns one dbITerm per master pin. Each dbITerm points to its dbMTerm (giving the pin's direction and shapes) and to the dbNet it connects, if any. A dbNet holds its set of dbITerms and dbBTerms. So to list the sinks of net n1, iterate the net's ITerms, keep those whose master terminal is an input, and read each one's instance. To get a cell's width, ask its master, not the instance: the instance stores only location, orientation and placement status. Engines that need to react to edits register a callback object on the block and are told when instances move or terminals connect. The Tcl and Python interfaces expose the same objects, so scripts can walk the database exactly as C++ code does.

## Flat blocks, wires and checkpoints

In the usual OpenROAD flow the block is flat: a hierarchical Verilog netlist is linked into a single level of leaf instances, with hierarchy preserved in names and, in recent versions, optional module objects. Connectivity and geometry are distinct objects: a dbNet is logical connectivity that exists from synthesis onward, while a dbWire, written by the detailed router, encodes the routed shapes and vias. Power and ground live as special nets, from DEF SPECIALNETS, with special wires for stripes and rails. Finally, OpenDB has a native binary file format. Saving it between flow stages, as OpenROAD-flow-scripts does, keeps every object and property and reloads far faster than DEF, which is an interchange format with a fixed vocabulary. A stage that crashes can be rerun from the previous checkpoint.

## Going deeper

The OpenDB documentation and source in the OpenROAD repository (src/odb); Ajayi et al., "Toward an Open-Source Digital Flow: First Learnings from the OpenROAD Project", DAC 2019.

problems.q:
In OpenDB, what object represents one instance's connection point for one pin of its master?

A) dbBTerm

B) dbMTerm

C) dbNet

D) dbITerm
problems.a: dbITerm
problems.e: A dbMTerm is a pin of the master cell, a dbBTerm is a port of the block, and a dbITerm is the instance-specific terminal that a dbNet connects to.

problems.q:
Where does OpenDB keep a metal layer's direction, pitch and minimum width?

A) In a dbTechLayer under dbTech

B) In each dbInst

C) In the dbBlock's rows

D) In each dbNet
problems.a: In a dbTechLayer under dbTech
problems.e: Layer rules are technology data, read from technology LEF into dbTech and its dbTechLayer objects.

problems.q:
OpenDB's schema closely follows which industry formats?

A) LEF and DEF

B) SPEF and SDF

C) GDSII and OASIS

D) Liberty and SDC
problems.a: LEF and DEF
problems.e: OpenDB was designed around LEF/DEF concepts: technology layers, sites, macros, pins, components, nets, special nets and wires.

problems.q:
A plug-in reads a dbInst's location and wants the cell's width. Where does the width come from?

A) The net the instance drives

B) The block's DIEAREA

C) The instance's dbMaster

D) The instance's dbITerms
problems.a: The instance's dbMaster
problems.e: Size, pins and obstructions belong to the master. The instance stores placement, orientation and status.

problems.q:
Which OpenDB object represents a port at the boundary of the block, such as a top-level input?

A) dbITerm

B) dbMTerm

C) dbBTerm

D) dbRow
problems.a: dbBTerm
problems.e: A block terminal belongs to the block, connects to a net and may have pin shapes placed on the boundary by pin placement.

problems.q:
A script wants every sink of net n1. Which traversal does the OpenDB object model support directly?

A) From the dbNet to its dbITerms, then each dbITerm to its dbInst

B) From the dbBlock's rows to the net

C) From dbTech to the net's layers

D) From the dbNet to its dbMaster
problems.a: From the dbNet to its dbITerms, then each dbITerm to its dbInst
problems.e: A net owns the set of instance terminals it connects. Each terminal knows its instance and its master terminal, which gives the pin direction.

problems.q:
OpenDB is a database of a single flattened block for most flows. What does a hierarchical Verilog netlist become when it is read in the usual OpenROAD flow?

A) A GDS hierarchy

B) A set of DEF files, one per module

C) One block per Verilog module, all fully linked

D) A flat block, with hierarchy kept only in instance names or optional hierarchy objects
problems.a: A flat block, with hierarchy kept only in instance names or optional hierarchy objects
problems.e: Physical design in OpenROAD operates on a flat netlist. Hierarchical names survive, and newer support can retain module hierarchy, but the engines work on flat instances.

problems.q:
Why does OpenDB distinguish dbWire from dbNet?

A) A wire is a net with only two pins

B) A net stores timing, a wire stores names

C) Wires are only for clock nets

D) A net is logical connectivity; a wire is its routed geometry
problems.a: A net is logical connectivity; a wire is its routed geometry
problems.e: Connectivity exists before routing. The wire, written by the detailed router, encodes the shapes and vias that realize it.

problems.q:
Special nets in OpenDB, from DEF SPECIALNETS, usually hold what?

A) Clock nets after CTS

B) Scan chains

C) Power and ground nets with their stripes and rails

D) Nets with timing exceptions
problems.a: Power and ground nets with their stripes and rails
problems.e: SPECIALNETS describe nets routed with special, usually prescribed geometry: power grids, rings and followpin rails.

lesson:
# Memory footprint of a netlist

A modern block can have tens of millions of instances and over a hundred million terminals, so bytes per object decide whether a design fits in memory and how fast engines sweep it. Estimating a footprint is simple arithmetic over object counts and record sizes, but the record sizes depend on choices a tool designer makes: pointer width, padding, and what is stored inline. This lesson sizes a netlist, compares pointers with indices and computes padded record sizes.

## Counting bytes per object

Footprint is the sum over object kinds of count times record size. Take 1,000,000 instances of 64 bytes, 1,100,000 nets of 48 bytes, and 3.2 ITerms per instance at 24 bytes each. Instances take $64 \times 10^6$ bytes, nets $52.8 \times 10^6$ bytes, ITerms $3.2 \times 10^6 \times 24 = 76.8 \times 10^6$ bytes, for 193.6 MB. ITerms dominate because they are the most numerous objects, so shaving 4 bytes from the ITerm record saves more than shaving 16 from the instance. The estimate is linear in design size, $O(n)$, but the constant matters: a 20-fold larger design at the same density needs about 3.9 GB for these objects alone, before names, wires, timing graphs and engine-private data, which together often exceed the netlist itself.

## Indices instead of pointers

On a 64-bit machine a pointer takes 8 bytes. A reference stored as a 32-bit index into a per-type table takes 4, and 32 bits can address over 4 billion objects of one kind, more than any block needs. An ITerm typically references its instance, its master terminal, its net and neighbours in per-net or per-instance lists. With 4 references per ITerm and 10 million ITerms, switching from pointers to indices saves $10^7 \times 4 \times 4 = 160$ MB. Indices bring further benefits: the table can grow and move in memory without breaking references, the tables can be written to disk and read back without pointer fix-up, and a side array indexed by the same number can attach engine data to every object. The cost is one extra addition per access, base plus index times size, which is almost always free next to the cache misses it prevents.

## Alignment and padding

A C++ compiler aligns each field to a multiple of its size and rounds the record up to a multiple of its largest field, so field order changes the size. Take fields flags (1 byte), master (8), x (4), orient (1), net (8). In that order, flags sits at 0, master is padded to 8, x at 16, orient at 20, net is padded to 24 and ends at 32: the record is 32 bytes, of which 22 are payload and 10 are padding. Sorted from largest to smallest, master, net, x, flags, orient end at 22 and round up to 24 bytes. Saving 8 bytes on a record repeated 10 million times is 80 MB. Database authors also pack flags into bit fields, store coordinates as 32-bit integers in database units rather than doubles, and keep variable-size data such as names out of line.

## Going deeper

Ulrich Drepper, "What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory" (2007); the OpenDB source in the OpenROAD repository for its object tables.

problems.q: A netlist database stores each instance in 56 bytes, each net in 72 bytes and each ITerm in 24 bytes. The design has 900000 instances with an average of 2.5 ITerms each, and 990000 nets. How much memory do these objects take, in megabytes (1 MB = 10^6 bytes)? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Instances: 900000 x 56 = 50400000 bytes. Nets: 990000 x 72 = 71280000 bytes. ITerms: 2250000 x 24 = 54000000 bytes. Total 175680000 bytes, which is 175.7 MB.

problems.q: A netlist database stores each instance in 48 bytes, each net in 32 bytes and each ITerm in 16 bytes. The design has 600000 instances with an average of 3 ITerms each, and 720000 nets. How much memory do these objects take, in megabytes (1 MB = 10^6 bytes)? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Instances: 600000 x 48 = 28800000 bytes. Nets: 720000 x 32 = 23040000 bytes. ITerms: 1800000 x 16 = 28800000 bytes. Total 80640000 bytes, which is 80.6 MB.

problems.q: A netlist database stores each instance in 64 bytes, each net in 32 bytes and each ITerm in 20 bytes. The design has 1300000 instances with an average of 3.7 ITerms each, and 1300000 nets. How much memory do these objects take, in megabytes (1 MB = 10^6 bytes)? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Instances: 1300000 x 64 = 83200000 bytes. Nets: 1300000 x 32 = 41600000 bytes. ITerms: 4810000 x 20 = 96200000 bytes. Total 221000000 bytes, which is 221 MB.

If every reference is stored as a 32-bit index into an object table instead of a 64-bit pointer, how much memory is saved, in megabytes (1 MB = 10^6 bytes)? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Each reference shrinks from 8 to 4 bytes, saving 4 bytes: 5000000 ITerms x 5 references x 4 bytes = 100 MB. Indices also survive reallocation of the table and serialize without pointer fix-up.

If every reference is stored as a 32-bit index into an object table instead of a 64-bit pointer, how much memory is saved, in megabytes (1 MB = 10^6 bytes)? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Each reference shrinks from 8 to 4 bytes, saving 4 bytes: 14000000 ITerms x 4 references x 4 bytes = 224 MB. Indices also survive reallocation of the table and serialize without pointer fix-up.

problems.q: A C++ record declares its fields in this order: weight (8 bytes), master (8 bytes), y (4 bytes), status (2 bytes). Each field is aligned to a multiple of its own size, and the record size is rounded up to a multiple of its largest field. What is the size of the record in bytes?
problems.e: Lay the fields out in order, padding each to its alignment: weight at 0, master at 8, y at 16, status at 20, ending at byte 22; rounding up to a multiple of 8 gives 24 bytes. Sorting the fields from largest to smallest would remove most of the padding, which matters when the record is repeated millions of times.

problems.e: Lay the fields out in order, padding each to its alignment: weight at 0, status at 8, level at 10, y at 12, flags at 16, net at 24, ending at byte 32; rounding up to a multiple of 8 gives 32 bytes. label: Cache locality and data-oriented layouts
lesson:
# Cache locality and data-oriented layouts

Placement, timing and routing engines spend most of their time in loops over millions of objects, and those loops are usually limited by memory traffic rather than arithmetic. Memory moves in cache lines, typically 64 bytes, so what matters is how many lines a loop touches. Data-oriented layout arranges data by how loops read it: arrays of structures, structures of arrays, or hot and cold splits. It is one of the cheapest large speedups available to a tool designer.

## Cache lines touched by a loop

A cache line is the unit the hardware fetches: read one byte and the whole 64-byte line comes in. Suppose 65,536 cells are stored as an array of 96-byte structs, and a density loop reads only each cell's 4-byte x coordinate. The structs are contiguous, so the loop sweeps the whole array: $65536 \times 96 = 6{,}291{,}456$ bytes, or 98,304 lines. Only 4 of every 96 bytes brought in are used, about 4%. If the structs were instead scattered across the heap, each accessed through its own pointer, every cell would cost at least one separate line, and the hardware prefetcher could not predict the next address, so each access might wait for main memory. Contiguity and density are the two levers: walk memory in order, and make the bytes you walk be the bytes you need.

## Structure of arrays

A structure of arrays stores each field in its own contiguous array: all x values together, all y values together, and so on. The same loop over x now reads $65536 \times 4 = 262{,}144$ bytes, 4,096 lines, instead of 98,304. The reduction factor is the struct size over the field size, $96 / 4 = 24$. Dense arrays of one type also let the compiler vectorize: one SIMD instruction can add a displacement to 8 x values at once. Electrostatic global placers keep cell positions, sizes and gradients in exactly this form, often as arrays of floats ready for vector units or GPUs. The cost is that code reading many fields of one object touches several arrays, and inserting or deleting an object must update every array, so the layout suits the hot inner loops more than the editing interface.

## Hot and cold splitting

A full structure of arrays is not always worth the disruption. A middle ground splits each object into a hot part, the few fields the inner loops read, and a cold part, everything else: names, property lists, rarely used flags. If the hot part is 16 bytes (x, y, width, a net index), a pass over 65,536 cells touches $65536 \times 16 / 64 = 16{,}384$ lines instead of 98,304, most of the gain of a full split while related fields stay together. The cold part is reached by the same index when needed. The same reasoning drives other choices: storing net terminals in one flat array with per-net offsets rather than a linked list per net, sorting cells by location so neighbours share lines, and keeping coordinates as 32-bit integers rather than 64-bit doubles. Measure first: a profiler that counts cache misses shows which loops are memory bound.

## Going deeper

Ulrich Drepper, "What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory" (2007); Richard Fabian, "Data-Oriented Design" (2018).

problems.q: A placer stores 28672 cells as an array of 72-byte structs (array of structures). Its inner loop reads only the 4-byte x coordinate of every cell, in order. Cache lines are 64 bytes and the array starts on a line boundary. How many distinct cache lines does one pass of the loop touch?

Cache lines are 64 bytes and the array starts on a line boundary. The struct is split into a structure of arrays, so all x coordinates sit in one contiguous array. By what factor does the number of cache lines the loop touches fall? Round to 2 decimal places.

label: Handles, arenas and memory management
lesson:
# Handles, arenas and memory management

An EDA database creates and deletes millions of small objects while several engines hold references to them. How memory is allocated and how references are represented decide speed, footprint and, above all, whether a deleted object can crash another engine. The standard toolkit is object tables with stable handles, generation counters, arenas and pools for short-lived data, and compaction at safe points. This lesson covers each and the failure each one prevents.

## Handles, tables and arenas

Instead of handing out raw pointers, a database stores objects of one kind in a table and hands out handles: the index of the slot, often with a generation number. A handle is half the size of a 64-bit pointer when it is 32 bits, and stays valid when the table grows and moves. When an object is deleted its slot goes on a free list and is reused; the slot's generation counter increments, so a stale handle carrying the old generation is detected instead of silently reading the new occupant. Short-lived data follows a different pattern. A router's search state for one net or a parser's temporary tokens can come from an arena: allocation is a pointer increment, objects lie contiguously, and the whole arena is released at once when the pass ends. General heap allocation per object is slower and scatters objects across memory.

## Dangling references and leaks

Two failures dominate. A dangling reference arises when an engine keeps a raw pointer to an object that is later moved or freed. If a legalizer caches pointers into a vector of cells and the database then grows that vector, every cached pointer names the old storage, and reads become undefined behaviour that may pass tests and crash in production. Handles with validity checks, or storage that never moves objects, prevent it. A leak is memory never returned. Leaks look harmless per call but accumulate in long loops: 200 bytes per ECO iteration over 2,000,000 iterations is 400 MB. Agent-driven flows that run thousands of incremental edits in one session make both failures more likely, so long-running engines need leak tests and sanitizers in their regression suites, not only correct results on single runs.

## Compaction, side arrays and sharing

Deletion leaves holes. After deleting 30% of nets, a loop over the net table skips many empty slots, and density suffers. Compaction moves live objects together and remaps handles, which is only safe at a point where no engine holds old handles, or with a published old-to-new mapping. Engines often attach their own data through side arrays indexed by object number, such as a per-net criticality; when a net is created, each owner must grow its side array, usually in response to a creation callback. Sharing across threads is simplest when the database is frozen during a parallel phase: reading immutable data needs no locks, while reference counting every object makes threads contend on atomic counters. Finally, expect freed memory to stay in the process: allocators keep freed pages for reuse, so resident size may not fall when a design is closed.

## Going deeper

The OpenDB source in the OpenROAD repository (its dbTable and object id scheme); Richard Fabian, "Data-Oriented Design" (2018), the chapter on existence-based processing.

problems.q:
A database hands out object references as 32-bit indices into per-type tables instead of raw pointers. Which benefit follows directly?

A) References stay valid when a table is reallocated and are half the size

B) Objects can never be deleted

C) Lookups no longer need memory

D) Indices make multithreading automatic
problems.a: References stay valid when a table is reallocated and are half the size
problems.e: An index is relative to the table, so growing the table moves memory without breaking references, and a 32-bit index is half a 64-bit pointer.

problems.q:
A table reuses the slot of a deleted object. A stale handle to the old object now points at a new one. What prevents the confusion?

A) A generation counter stored in the handle and the slot

B) Sorting the table

C) Larger indices

D) A mutex around every read
problems.a: A generation counter stored in the handle and the slot
problems.e: Each slot increments its generation on reuse. A handle carries the generation it was issued with, so a mismatch reveals a stale reference.

problems.q:
Why do EDA databases allocate millions of small objects from arenas or pools rather than one heap call each?

A) Arenas make objects immutable

B) Pools check design rules

C) The operating system forbids small allocations

D) Allocation is a pointer bump and objects of a kind stay contiguous
problems.a: Allocation is a pointer bump and objects of a kind stay contiguous
problems.e: General-purpose allocation has per-call overhead and scatters objects. Arenas cut both, which helps speed and cache locality.

problems.q:
Which data should be kept by value in a dense array rather than behind a pointer per element?

A) A per-design log file

B) Cell x and y coordinates read in every placement iteration

C) A rarely read property map per cell

D) The name string of each net
problems.a: Cell x and y coordinates read in every placement iteration
problems.e: Hot, small, fixed-size data belongs in contiguous arrays. Rarely used or variable-size data can live behind an indirection.

problems.q:
A legalizer stores raw pointers to cells in a vector, then the database grows its cell storage and moves objects. What happens?

A) The database refuses to grow

B) Nothing; pointers are relative

C) The pointers are updated automatically

D) The legalizer's pointers dangle and later reads are undefined behaviour
problems.a: The legalizer's pointers dangle and later reads are undefined behaviour
problems.e: Raw pointers name an address. When storage moves, they still name the old address. Stable handles or pointer-stable storage avoid this.

problems.q:
A legalizer stores raw pointers to cells in a vector, then the database grows its cell storage and moves objects. What happens?

A) The pointers are updated automatically

B) The database refuses to grow

C) Nothing; pointers are relative

D) The legalizer's pointers dangle and later reads are undefined behaviour
problems.a: The legalizer's pointers dangle and later reads are undefined behaviour
problems.e: Raw pointers name an address. When storage moves, they still name the old address. Stable handles or pointer-stable storage avoid this.

problems.q:
A tool frees a large design and the process memory stays high. What is the most likely reason?

A) The operating system leaks memory

B) The allocator keeps freed pages for reuse instead of returning them

C) The design was not really freed

D) Memory cannot be freed in C++
problems.a: The allocator keeps freed pages for reuse instead of returning them
problems.e: Allocators often retain freed memory in their own pools. Measured resident memory may fall only after the allocator trims or the process exits.

problems.q:
An engine keeps a derived per-net array indexed by net index. A new net is created. What must the engine do?

A) Grow its array to cover the new index before using it

B) Rebuild the whole database

C) Nothing; the array resizes itself in C++

D) Renumber every existing net
problems.a: Grow its array to cover the new index before using it
problems.e: Side arrays keyed by object index are cheap and cache friendly, but each owner must grow them, usually in response to a creation callback.

problems.q:
A tool frees a large design and the process memory stays high. What is the most likely reason?

A) Memory cannot be freed in C++

B) The allocator keeps freed pages for reuse instead of returning them

C) The design was not really freed

D) The operating system leaks memory
problems.a: The allocator keeps freed pages for reuse instead of returning them
problems.e: Allocators often retain freed memory in their own pools. Measured resident memory may fall only after the allocator trims or the process exits.

label: Serializing a design database
prereqs: Writing a number in another base
lesson:
# Serializing a design database

A tool must save its database between flow stages, ship it between machines and reload it quickly. Serialization turns the object tables into bytes, and its design decides file size and load time. Because databases are built on integer handles and coordinates in database units, compact integer encodings pay off directly: variable-length integers, delta encoding of sorted values and zigzag encoding of signed differences. These same encodings appear in many binary formats and checkpoint schemes.

## Variable-length integers

Most stored integers are small: pin indices, layer numbers, short offsets. A fixed 4-byte field wastes space on them. A variable-length integer (the LEB128 scheme) stores 7 payload bits per byte and uses the top bit as a continuation flag. A value below $2^7 = 128$ takes 1 byte, below $2^{14} = 16384$ takes 2, below $2^{21} = 2097152$ takes 3, and below $2^{28}$ takes 4. Example: the values 5, 300, 70000 and 3000000 take $1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10$ bytes, against 16 at fixed width. Decoding reads bytes until one has its top bit clear, shifting each 7-bit group into place. The format is self-delimiting, so no length field is needed, but it cannot be indexed randomly: to find the tenth value the reader must decode the first nine, which is why files add offset tables for random access.

## Delta encoding sorted coordinates

Coordinates are large numbers in database units, but sorted coordinates are close to each other. Delta encoding stores the first value and then each difference from the previous one. The x positions of cells in a row, 412000, 412380, 412760, 414280 and 416180, become 412000, 380, 380, 1520 and 1900. As variable-length integers these take $3 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 11$ bytes, against $5 \times 4 = 20$ bytes fixed, a saving of 9 bytes. Over millions of cells, routing segments or polygon vertices the savings are large, and general compressors do even better on the regular deltas that result. The method depends on order: the writer must sort first, or choose an order such as row by row in which neighbours are close, and the reader must decode sequentially to rebuild absolute values.

## Zigzag encoding signed deltas

Differences are not always positive: polygon vertices go back and forth, and wires turn. A negative number in two's complement has its high bits set, so as an unsigned variable-length integer it would take the maximum number of bytes. Zigzag encoding maps signed integers to unsigned ones so that small magnitudes stay small: $n \mapsto 2n$ for $n \ge 0$ and $n \mapsto -2n - 1$ for $n < 0$. So 0, -1, 1, -2, 2 map to 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. Example: deltas 63, -64, 700 and -8192 map to 126, 127, 1400 and 16383, taking $1 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 6$ bytes. Note the boundaries: 64 maps to 128, which needs 2 bytes, while -64 maps to 127 and needs one. Binary database formats and GDS-like streams use these ideas, alongside versioned headers so that a newer reader can load an older file.

## Going deeper

The Protocol Buffers encoding documentation on varints and zigzag encoding; the OASIS format specification (SEMI P39), whose integer encoding uses the same ideas.

problems.q: A database writer stores unsigned integers as variable-length integers: 7 payload bits per byte, with the top bit of each byte marking that another byte follows. How many bytes does it write for the values 139317469, 9959452, 10430009, 174201510?
problems.e: A value below 2^7 = 128 takes 1 byte, below 2^14 = 16384 takes 2, below 2^21 = 2097152 takes 3, below 2^28 takes 4. Here 139317469 takes 4, 9959452 takes 4, 10430009 takes 4, 174201510 takes 4, for 16 bytes.

problems.q: A database writer stores unsigned integers as variable-length integers: 7 payload bits per byte, with the top bit of each byte marking that another byte follows. How many bytes does it write for the values 81877967, 64, 1651095, 10, 120, 6092?
problems.e: A value below 2^7 = 128 takes 1 byte, below 2^14 = 16384 takes 2, below 2^21 = 2097152 takes 3, below 2^28 takes 4. Here 81877967 takes 4, 64 takes 1, 1651095 takes 3, 10 takes 1, 120 takes 1, 6092 takes 2, for 12 bytes.

problems.q: A database writer stores unsigned integers as variable-length integers: 7 payload bits per byte, with the top bit of each byte marking that another byte follows. How many bytes does it write for the values 34046427, 126, 9526, 43, 90?

problems.q: The x coordinates of the cells in one row, in database units and sorted, are 111000, 112900, 128100, 128480, 129240, 129620. A writer stores the first value and then each difference from the previous value, all as variable-length integers (7 payload bits per byte). How many bytes does this save against storing every coordinate as a fixed 4-byte integer?
problems.e: Stored values: 111000 (3 B), 1900 (2 B), 15200 (2 B), 380 (2 B), 760 (2 B), 380 (2 B), 13 bytes in all, against 6 x 4 = 24 fixed. Saving: 11 bytes. Sorted coordinates have small gaps, which is why delta encoding pays.

problems.q: The x coordinates of the cells in one row, in database units and sorted, are 520000, 520190, 520760, 522660, 523230, 523420, 523610. A writer stores the first value and then each difference from the previous value, all as variable-length integers (7 payload bits per byte). How many bytes does this save against storing every coordinate as a fixed 4-byte integer?
problems.e: Stored values: 520000 (3 B), 190 (2 B), 570 (2 B), 1900 (2 B), 570 (2 B), 190 (2 B), 190 (2 B), 15 bytes in all, against 7 x 4 = 28 fixed. Saving: 13 bytes. Sorted coordinates have small gaps, which is why delta encoding pays.

problems.q: The x coordinates of the cells in one row, in database units and sorted, are 797000, 797190, 797570, 798140, 798520, 798900, 814100. A writer stores the first value and then each difference from the previous value, all as variable-length integers (7 payload bits per byte). How many bytes does this save against storing every coordinate as a fixed 4-byte integer?
problems.e: Stored values: 797000 (3 B), 190 (2 B), 380 (2 B), 570 (2 B), 380 (2 B), 380 (2 B), 15200 (2 B), 15 bytes in all, against 7 x 4 = 28 fixed. Saving: 13 bytes. Sorted coordinates have small gaps, which is why delta encoding pays.

problems.q: Signed coordinate deltas are written with zigzag encoding, which maps n to 2n when n is at least 0 and to -2n - 1 when n is negative, and the result is stored as a variable-length integer (7 payload bits per byte). How many bytes do the deltas -8192, 5, -20000, -64 take?
problems.e: -8192 maps to 16383 (2 B); 5 maps to 10 (1 B); -20000 maps to 39999 (3 B); -64 maps to 127 (1 B), for 7 bytes. Without zigzag, a negative number in two's complement would look huge and take the maximum number of bytes.

problems.q: Signed coordinate deltas are written with zigzag encoding, which maps n to 2n when n is at least 0 and to -2n - 1 when n is negative, and the result is stored as a variable-length integer (7 payload bits per byte). How many bytes do the deltas 8192, -1, -700, 100, -30 take?
problems.e: 8192 maps to 16384 (3 B); -1 maps to 1 (1 B); -700 maps to 1399 (2 B); 100 maps to 200 (2 B); -30 maps to 59 (1 B), for 9 bytes. Without zigzag, a negative number in two's complement would look huge and take the maximum number of bytes.

problems.q: Signed coordinate deltas are written with zigzag encoding, which maps n to 2n when n is at least 0 and to -2n - 1 when n is negative, and the result is stored as a variable-length integer (7 payload bits per byte). How many bytes do the deltas -1, 700, -1, -100, 700, 5, -8192 take?
problems.e: -1 maps to 1 (1 B); 700 maps to 1400 (2 B); -1 maps to 1 (1 B); -100 maps to 199 (2 B); 700 maps to 1400 (2 B); 5 maps to 10 (1 B); -8192 maps to 16383 (2 B), for 11 bytes. Without zigzag, a negative number in two's complement would look huge and take the maximum number of bytes.

label: Tcl evaluation and substitution
lesson:
# Tcl evaluation and substitution

Most EDA tools, OpenROAD and OpenSTA included, are driven by Tcl, and SDC constraint files are Tcl programs. Tcl's evaluation rules are short but unusual: everything is a string, a command is a list of words, and substitution happens once, before the command runs, in ways that braces and quotes control. Tool builders must know these rules to write command parsers, to read SDC correctly, and to avoid subtle scripting bugs such as integer division that differs from C.

## Words and lists

A Tcl command is a sequence of words separated by white space; the first word names the command. A Tcl list has the same syntax: elements separated by spaces, with braces grouping several words into one element. The command llength counts top-level elements. In the list u1 {a b c} u2 {} {x {y z}}, written inside outer braces, there are five elements: u1, the group a b c, u2, an empty element, and the group x {y z}. Nesting does not matter to llength; a braced group is one element however much it contains, and an empty pair of braces is a legal empty element. Tool commands that return collections of objects, such as the get commands of SDC, return lists or list-like handles, and scripts iterate them with foreach. A list built by string concatenation can split wrongly when names contain spaces, so scripts should build lists with the list command.

## Substitution in quotes and braces

Before a command runs, Tcl performs one round of substitution on each word: a dollar sign followed by a variable name is replaced by the variable's value, and a bracketed command such as [set w] is replaced by that command's result. Double quotes group a word but still allow substitution. Braces group a word and suppress all substitution. So after set w U42, the command set s "inst_[set w]/Z" stores inst_U42/Z, 10 characters, while set s {inst_[set w]/Z} stores the literal text inst_[set w]/Z, 14 characters. Substitution happens exactly once: if a value contains brackets, they are not evaluated again. This matters for EDA names, which often contain brackets for bus bits such as data[3]: a script must brace or escape them, or Tcl will try to run a command named 3.

## Integer arithmetic in expr

The expr command evaluates arithmetic. Its argument should be braced, as in expr {a + b} with variables, so that expr itself performs substitution once and can compile the expression; unbraced expressions are substituted twice and are slower and less safe. Integer division in Tcl rounds toward negative infinity, and the remainder takes the sign of the divisor, so that $a = b \cdot q + r$ always holds. Thus expr {17 / 5} is 3 and expr {17 % 5} is 2, but expr {-17 / 5} is -4 and expr {-17 % 5} is 3, and expr {17 % -5} is -3. C and C++ truncate toward zero instead, giving -3 and -2 for the negative cases. A grid-snapping formula ported from C++ to a Tcl script can therefore snap negative coordinates differently. Mixing in a floating-point operand, as in 7 / 2.0, gives 3.5.

## Going deeper

John Ousterhout and Ken Jones, "Tcl and the Tk Toolkit" (2nd ed., 2009), the chapters on syntax and expressions; the Tcl manual page Tcl(n), which states the evaluation rules.

problems.q: In Tcl, which value does the command `llength {{a {met2 c}} {b a} {} {}}` return?
problems.e: llength counts top-level elements. A braced group, however much it contains and even when empty, is one element, so the list {{a {met2 c}} {b a} {} {}} has 4 elements.

problems.q: In Tcl, which value does the command `llength {{b {u1 x}} {c {met1 c}} {c clk} met2 {a {u2 n12}}}` return?
problems.e: llength counts top-level elements. A braced group, however much it contains and even when empty, is one element, so the list {{b {u1 x}} {c {met1 c}} {c clk} met2 {a {u2 n12}}} has 5 elements.

problems.q: In Tcl, which value does the command `llength {{core met1} {} a u1 {n12 {core u2}}}` return?
problems.e: llength counts top-level elements. A braced group, however much it contains and even when empty, is one element, so the list {{core met1} {} a u1 {n12 {core u2}}} has 5 elements.

problems.q: A Tcl script runs `set w reg_a` and then `set s {pin:[set w]/Z}`. Which value does `string length [set s]` return?
problems.e: Inside braces Tcl performs no substitution, so s holds the literal text pin:[set w]/Z, which has 13 characters.

problems.q: A Tcl script runs `set w clk_div` and then `set s "inst_[set w]_q"`. Which value does `string length [set s]` return?
problems.e: Inside double quotes Tcl performs command substitution, so [set w] is replaced by clk_div and s becomes inst_clk_div_q, which has 14 characters.

problems.q: A Tcl script runs `set w reg_a` and then `set s {inst_[set w]_q}`. Which value does `string length [set s]` return?
problems.e: Inside braces Tcl performs no substitution, so s holds the literal text inst_[set w]_q, which has 14 characters.

problems.q: In Tcl, which value does `expr {-17 % 9}` return?
problems.e: Tcl integer division rounds toward negative infinity, so -17 / 9 = -2, and the remainder -17 % 9 = 1 has the sign of the divisor, keeping a = b x quotient + remainder: 9 x -2 + 1 = -17. C and C++ truncate toward zero instead, a classic porting bug.

problems.q: In Tcl, which value does `expr {-45 % 6}` return?
problems.e: Tcl integer division rounds toward negative infinity, so -45 / 6 = -8, and the remainder -45 % 6 = 3 has the sign of the divisor, keeping a = b x quotient + remainder: 6 x -8 + 3 = -45. C and C++ truncate toward zero instead, a classic porting bug.

problems.q: In Tcl, which value does `expr {-7 / 8}` return?
problems.e: Tcl integer division rounds toward negative infinity, so -7 / 8 = -1, and the remainder -7 % 8 = 1 has the sign of the divisor, keeping a = b x quotient + remainder: 8 x -1 + 1 = -7. C and C++ truncate toward zero instead, a classic porting bug.

label: Tcl and Python tool APIs
lesson:
# Tcl and Python tool APIs

EDA engines are written in C++ for speed, but users and flows drive them from scripts. OpenROAD exposes its engines and its OpenDB database through a Tcl shell and through Python. The scripting layer is how flows are built, how reports are customized and, increasingly, how agents call tools. Designing that layer well decides what can be automated cheaply, what must be compiled, and how safe and reproducible scripted runs are.

## Scripting shells over compiled engines

In a modern EDA tool the command language is a thin layer. A global-placement command typed in the OpenROAD Tcl shell parses its options and calls into the C++ placer, which reads and edits the shared database; no placement arithmetic happens in Tcl. Tcl has stayed the industry's command language because it is small and easy to embed in a C or C++ program, and because SDC, the constraint language, is Tcl. Python is the second interface: OpenROAD can run with a Python interpreter and expose the database objects and engine calls, which suits data analysis and machine-learning experiments. The bindings are usually generated rather than handwritten: a wrapper generator such as SWIG reads interface descriptions of the C++ classes and emits glue code for each language, so one C++ API serves both.

## What to script and what to compile

Every call from a script into C++ crosses a boundary that costs far more than a simple getter. A Python loop that calls one location getter on each of 2,000,000 instances pays that overhead 2,000,000 times and can take minutes, while the same loop in C++ takes milliseconds. The rule follows: scripts orchestrate, configure and report; inner loops are compiled. A custom report of nets with more than 50 sinks and their drivers is a script over the database API. A new detailed-placement move evaluated millions of times is a compiled extension. Between the two sit bulk calls: a command that returns all locations at once, or that accepts a whole list of objects, moves the loop into C++ while keeping the script in control. Good APIs offer such bulk operations for the queries users run most.

## Designing a script API

Several rules separate a robust script API from a fragile one. Commands should accept and return object handles or collections rather than names, so a script does not convert 100,000 objects to strings and look each up again. Handles must be validated: if a script holds a handle to a net that another command deleted, the API should raise a script error rather than read freed memory. Configuration should travel as explicit command options or configuration objects, not as global variables whose last writer wins, so that each call is reproducible and loggable. C++ exceptions must be caught at the boundary and turned into script errors. When the caller is an agent rather than a person, the same rules matter more: typed, documented commands that return structured results can be called and parsed reliably, while free-text reports must be scraped and break when wording changes.

## Going deeper

The OpenROAD documentation on its Tcl and Python interfaces; the SWIG documentation; John Ousterhout, "Scripting: Higher-Level Programming for the 21st Century", IEEE Computer, 1998.

problems.q:
OpenROAD exposes its engines through a Tcl shell. What does a typical Tcl command such as a global-placement command do underneath?

A) Calls into the C++ engine, which reads and edits the shared database

B) Interprets a placement algorithm written in Tcl

C) Sends the design to a remote server

D) Writes a DEF file and launches a separate placer binary
problems.a: Calls into the C++ engine, which reads and edits the shared database
problems.e: The Tcl layer is a thin command interface. The compiled engine does the work on the in-memory database, so scripting costs almost nothing at run time.

problems.q:
How are C++ database classes usually made callable from Tcl and Python in open EDA tools?

A) A wrapper generator produces bindings from the C++ headers or interface files

B) The scripts parse the C++ source at run time

C) The C++ code is compiled to Tcl bytecode

D) Each class is rewritten by hand in both languages
problems.a: A wrapper generator produces bindings from the C++ headers or interface files
problems.e: Tools such as SWIG generate glue code that maps C++ classes and methods to script objects, so one C++ API serves several languages.

problems.q:
Besides Tcl, what scripting interface does OpenROAD offer for working with its database and engines?

A) No other interface; Tcl is the only way in

B) A Python interface to the same engines and database objects

C) A Perl interface only for reports

D) A JavaScript interface running in a browser
problems.a: A Python interface to the same engines and database objects
problems.e: OpenROAD can run with a Python interpreter, giving access to the database objects and engine calls, which suits data analysis and machine-learning work.

problems.q:
A Tcl procedure stores a database object handle in a variable, then a command deletes that net. The procedure later uses the handle. What should a well-designed API do?

A) Detect that the object is gone and raise a script error

B) Crash the tool as intended

C) Recreate the net

D) Silently return data from the deleted net
problems.a: Detect that the object is gone and raise a script error
problems.e: Script handles must be validated, or a stale handle becomes a use-after-free inside the C++ engine.

problems.q:
Which task needs a compiled C++ extension rather than a script?

A) Printing a summary of utilization

B) Selecting which corner to analyze

C) Reading a configuration file of 20 parameters

D) A new detailed-placement move evaluated millions of times
problems.a: A new detailed-placement move evaluated millions of times
problems.e: Inner-loop work runs millions of times and must be compiled. Scripts orchestrate and configure; they should not sit in hot loops.

problems.q:
A Tcl procedure stores a database object handle in a variable, then a command deletes that net. The procedure later uses the handle. What should a well-designed API do?

A) Recreate the net

B) Crash the tool as intended

C) Detect that the object is gone and raise a script error

D) Silently return data from the deleted net
problems.a: Detect that the object is gone and raise a script error
problems.e: Script handles must be validated, or a stale handle becomes a use-after-free inside the C++ engine.

problems.q:
A tool exposes a Python API and an agent will drive it. Which property of the API matters most for the agent?

A) Commands that print human-only text

B) As many commands as possible

C) Short command names

D) Typed, documented calls that return structured results
problems.a: Typed, documented calls that return structured results
problems.e: An agent needs to know argument types and to parse the result. Free-text output must be scraped and breaks when wording changes.

problems.q:
Two scripts set the same global Tcl variable to configure an engine, and results depend on which ran last. What API change fixes this?

A) Pass configuration as explicit command options or a config object

B) Rename the variable

C) Run the scripts in a random order

D) Store the variable in DEF
problems.a: Pass configuration as explicit command options or a config object
problems.e: Hidden global state makes runs order-dependent. Explicit parameters make each call reproducible and easy to log.

problems.q:
A Tcl command returns a list of 100,000 object names as one string, and the script then looks each name up again. What design would avoid the waste?

A) Write the names to a file

B) Return a longer string

C) Return object handles or a collection that commands accept directly

D) Require the user to type the names
problems.a: Return object handles or a collection that commands accept directly
problems.e: Name round-trips cost string building and hashing. Collections of handles, as in SDC-style get commands, pass objects without re-lookup.

label: Domain-specific languages for EDA
lesson:
# Domain-specific languages for EDA

EDA is full of small languages: SDC for constraints, Liberty for cell libraries, UPF for power intent, rule decks for DRC and LVS, synthesis scripts, and flow configuration files. A tool designer must decide, for each new kind of input, whether it is an embedded language hosted in Tcl or Python, or an external declarative format with its own parser, and how it will be validated. Those choices decide what users can express and what tools can analyze.

## Embedded and external DSLs

An embedded DSL adds domain commands to a host language. SDC is the classic case: create_clock and set_input_delay are commands run by a Tcl interpreter inside the timer, so SDC inherits Tcl variables, loops and procedures. UPF and many flow scripts follow the same pattern. An external DSL has its own grammar and parser. Liberty is one: groups and attributes describing cells, with no variables or loops. Declarative configuration in YAML or JSON is another. Embedding is cheap to build and powerful to use, because the host language provides parsing, expressions and control flow for free. External declarative formats are easier to analyze: a tool can validate them against a schema, compare two versions, or generate them from a program without running any code. Yosys scripts sit between, as a command language that names passes in a registry and orders them.

## Validation and semantic checks

A DSL is only as good as its error reporting. Syntax errors are found by the parser, but most real mistakes are semantic: a clock with a negative period, a delay on a port that does not exist, a misspelled configuration key. Semantic checks belong where the context is known, when the command executes or the key is read, and they should name the file and line. Silent defaults are the worst failure: a flow configuration with PLACE_DENSTY misspelled that quietly uses the default density produces wrong results with no error. Declaring a schema, the known keys with their types and ranges, and rejecting unknown keys turns such typos into immediate failures. The same discipline makes a DSL safe to accept from automated sources: an agent proposing flow parameters through a validated schema can only touch the intended knobs.

## Analyzing and trusting DSL programs

The power of an embedded DSL limits what can be known without running it. An SDC file that uses a Tcl loop to generate 10,000 false-path commands has those commands only after evaluation, so a static checker must execute the Tcl, or a restricted subset of it, to see them. A declarative rule language, by contrast, exposes its structure, letting an engine reorder rules, share work among them and run them in parallel. Trust is the other issue. A full Tcl interpreter can execute shell commands, open files and sockets; when input may come from an agent or another team, the tool needs a safe interpreter or a restricted command set. Finally, the meaning of a configuration key can change between tool versions. Versioning the schema and recording it with every run lets a regression explain why the same input gave different results.

## Going deeper

Martin Fowler, "Domain-Specific Languages" (2010); the Synopsys Design Constraints format documentation; the Liberty reference manual's description of its syntax.

problems.q:
Liberty has its own grammar of groups and attributes and no loops or variables. What kind of language is it?

A) A hardware description language

B) An external declarative data language

C) An embedded scripting language

D) A general-purpose programming language
problems.a: An external declarative data language
problems.e: Liberty is declarative data with a dedicated parser. It describes cells; it does not compute.

problems.q:
What is the main advantage of an embedded DSL over an external one for tool configuration?

A) It needs no documentation

B) It is always faster to execute

C) It cannot have syntax errors

D) It reuses the host language's parser, variables and control flow
problems.a: It reuses the host language's parser, variables and control flow
problems.e: Embedding gives loops, procedures and expressions for free. The cost is that users can write arbitrary code, which is harder to analyze.

problems.q:
What is the main advantage of a declarative external DSL such as a YAML or JSON flow configuration?

A) A tool can validate and diff it without executing anything

B) It can express any computation

C) It runs faster than compiled code

D) It removes the need for a schema
problems.a: A tool can validate and diff it without executing anything
problems.e: Declarative data can be checked against a schema, compared between runs and generated by programs safely.

problems.q:
A flow config has the key PLACE_DENSTY (misspelled). The flow silently uses the default density. What DSL design choice would catch it?

A) Make all keys optional

B) Store config in environment variables

C) Reject unknown keys against a declared schema

D) Accept any key for flexibility
problems.a: Reject unknown keys against a declared schema
problems.e: Silently ignoring unknown keys turns typos into wrong results. A schema with known keys and types fails fast.

problems.q:
A Yosys synthesis script is a sequence of named passes with options. What does that make it?

A) A command language over a pass registry

B) A layout description

C) A timing constraint language

D) A netlist format
problems.a: A command language over a pass registry
problems.e: Each command names a registered pass that transforms the design in RTLIL. The script orders the passes.

problems.q:
A user writes create_clock with a period of -2 in an SDC file. When should a well-designed reader report it?

A) Only after timing analysis finishes

B) Only at tape-out

C) Never; negative periods are legal

D) When the command executes, with the file and line
problems.a: When the command executes, with the file and line
problems.e: Semantic checks belong at the command, where the context is known, so the user can fix the source line.

problems.q:
Two versions of a tool interpret the same configuration key differently. What practice prevents silent changes in results?

A) Version the schema and record it with every run

B) Let each user decide

C) Never change the tool

D) Remove the key
problems.a: Version the schema and record it with every run
problems.e: A versioned schema makes changes explicit, and recording it with results lets a regression explain a difference.

problems.q:
An SDC file uses Tcl loops to generate 10,000 set_false_path commands. A static checker without a Tcl interpreter must report all exceptions. What does it need?

A) Only the first line

B) The Liberty file

C) To execute the Tcl, because the commands exist only after evaluation

D) Only a regular-expression scan of the file
problems.a: To execute the Tcl, because the commands exist only after evaluation
problems.e: In an embedded DSL the effective commands are the result of running the program. A pure text scan cannot see generated commands.

problems.q:
A DSL for design rules lets authors write each rule as a declarative expression. What does that let the engine do that imperative scripts would not?

A) Skip checking rules

B) Run without a layout

C) Avoid storing geometry

D) Analyze, reorder and batch rules for efficient evaluation
problems.a: Analyze, reorder and batch rules for efficient evaluation
problems.e: Declarative rules expose their structure, so the engine can share work across rules and run them in parallel.

label: Parsing structural Verilog netlists
prereqs: Netlists as the shared currency of the flow
lesson:
# Parsing structural Verilog netlists

After synthesis, a design travels as a structural Verilog netlist: a module with ports, wire declarations and instances of library cells. Every back-end tool starts by parsing this text into its object model, turning ports into block terminals, instances into instance objects, and each connection into an instance terminal on a net. A tool designer must know exactly what the text implies, because a mis-parsed connection silently becomes a wrong circuit.

## Instances, nets and terminals in the text

Read `module top (a, b, y0); input a, b; output y0; wire n1; NAND2_X1 u1 (.A1(a), .A2(b), .ZN(n1)); INV_X1 u2 (.A(n1), .ZN(y0)); endmodule`. The parser creates two instances, u1 and u2. Each port becomes a block terminal (BTerm) and also names a net, so the nets are a, b, y0 and the wire n1: four nets. Each instance pin becomes an instance terminal (ITerm): u1 has three pins and u2 two, so five ITerms. A useful invariant for a netlist where every cell has one output: each instance drives exactly one net, so the net count is the number of primary inputs plus the number of instances. If the count from the parser disagrees, something was dropped or duplicated.

## Fanout from named connections

A named connection `.A2(n1)` binds pin A2 of the instance to net n1, whatever order the connections are written in. The parser looks up A2 on the cell master, finds its direction from the library, and attaches an ITerm to n1. The fanout of a net is the number of input pins it drives. In `NAND2_X1 u3 (.A1(n1), .A2(n1), .ZN(n2)); INV_X1 u4 (.A(n1), .ZN(y0));`, net n1 drives u3/A1, u3/A2 and u4/A: fanout 3, even though only two instances read it, because each pin is a separate sink. Output pins such as ZN are drivers and are not counted. Fanout feeds everything downstream: load capacitance for timing, net weights for placement, and buffering decisions.

## Positional connections need the cell's port order

Verilog also allows positional connections: `NAND2_X1 u5 (n1, b, n3);` binds signals to ports in the order the cell's module declares them. The netlist alone cannot tell you which signal is the output: the parser needs the port order, from a Verilog cell library or from the order the tool assumes for the master. If NAND2_X1 is declared as (A1, A2, ZN), then n1 is A1, b is A2 and n3 is the output ZN. Get the order wrong and the parser silently turns an output into an input, creating a net with two drivers and a dangling sink. Robust readers therefore check that every net has exactly one driver after reading, and treat positional connections to cells without a declared port order as an error. Escaped identifiers such as `\bus[3] ` (a backslash name ended by whitespace) are another trap for hand-written lexers.

## Going deeper

IEEE Std 1364-2005, the Verilog standard, sections on module instantiation; the Yosys manual on reading and writing netlists; the OpenROAD documentation for read_verilog and link_design.

problems.q: A parser reads this netlist into a design database: `module top (a, b, c, y0, y1, y2, y3, y4); input a, b, c; output y0, y1, y2, y3, y4; wire n1; AOI21_X1 u1 (.A(b), .B1(b), .B2(a), .ZN(y0)); AOI21_X1 u2 (.A(c), .B1(b), .B2(b), .ZN(n1)); NAND2_X1 u3 (.A1(b), .A2(b), .ZN(y1)); AND2_X1 u4 (.A1(c), .A2(b), .ZN(y2)); BUF_X1 u5 (.A(n1), .Z(y3)); INV_X1 u6 (.A(n1), .ZN(y4)); endmodule` How many nets does the block contain? Count every distinct signal, ports included.
problems.e: Each port is also a net: 3 inputs and 5 outputs, plus 1 declared wires, gives 9 nets. Every instance drives exactly one net here, so the count is inputs plus instances.

problems.q: A parser reads this netlist into a design database: `module top (a, b, c, y0, y1, y2); input a, b, c; output y0, y1, y2; wire n1; AOI21_X1 u1 (.A(c), .B1(a), .B2(a), .ZN(n1)); INV_X1 u2 (.A(n1), .ZN(y0)); AOI21_X1 u3 (.A(c), .B1(n1), .B2(c), .ZN(y1)); AND2_X1 u4 (.A1(n1), .A2(c), .ZN(y2)); endmodule` How many instance terminals (ITerms) does it create? Count one per pin of every instance, inputs and outputs.
problems.e: One ITerm per instance pin: u1 has 4, u2 has 2, u3 has 4, u4 has 3, for 13 in all. Ports become BTerms, not ITerms.

problems.q: A parser reads this netlist into a design database: `module top (a, b, c, d, y0); input a, b, c, d; output y0; wire n1, n2, n3; NAND3_X1 u1 (.A1(d), .A2(a), .A3(c), .ZN(n1)); AND2_X1 u2 (.A1(c), .A2(c), .ZN(n2)); NOR2_X1 u3 (.A1(c), .A2(n2), .ZN(n3)); AOI21_X1 u4 (.A(n3), .B1(n2), .B2(n1), .ZN(y0)); endmodule` How many nets does the block contain? Count every distinct signal, ports included.
