Instead of recomputing in each callback, it sets a dirty flag and recomputes once at the next timing query, and only if the flag is set. The session runs: instance moved, QUERY, instance created, QUERY, pin connected or disconnected, pin connected or disconnected, instance created. How many times does the timer recompute?
problems.e: An eager timer would recompute on each of the 5 relevant callbacks. The lazy one recomputes only at queries that find the flag set, which happens 2 times.

problems.q: A timer subscribes to master swapped and pin connected or disconnected. Instead of recomputing in each callback, it sets a dirty flag and recomputes once at the next timing query, and only if the flag is set. The session runs: pin connected or disconnected, QUERY, QUERY, pin connected or disconnected, QUERY, instance moved, master swapped, pin connected or disconnected, QUERY. How many times does the timer recompute?
problems.e: An eager timer would recompute on each of the 4 relevant callbacks. The lazy one recomputes only at queries that find the flag set, which happens 3 times.

problems.q: A timer subscribes to instance moved and instance created. Instead of recomputing in each callback, it sets a dirty flag and recomputes once at the next timing query, and only if the flag is set. The session runs: instance created, pin connected or disconnected, QUERY, instance moved, QUERY, instance moved. How many times does the timer recompute?
problems.e: An eager timer would recompute on each of the 3 relevant callbacks. The lazy one recomputes only at queries that find the flag set, which happens 2 times.

problems.q: A database batches notifications: at each commit, every observer subscribed to at least one edit kind in the transaction gets exactly one call carrying the list of edits. Observers: the global router subscribes to instance moved, pin connected or disconnected and instance created; the density map subscribes to master swapped and instance created; the parasitic estimator subscribes to master swapped and instance created. The optimizer commits transaction 1: instance moved, master swapped, instance moved; transaction 2: instance created, pin connected or disconnected, master swapped; transaction 3: instance created, master swapped, instance moved, pin connected or disconnected. How many observer calls does the database make?
problems.e: Per transaction, count the observers touched at least once: 3 + 3 + 3, total 9. Per-edit notification would have made 17 calls.

problems.q: A database batches notifications: at each commit, every observer subscribed to at least one edit kind in the transaction gets exactly one call carrying the list of edits. Observers: the power analyzer subscribes to instance moved; the timer subscribes to master swapped, pin connected or disconnected and instance created; the density map subscribes to instance created; the parasitic estimator subscribes to instance moved, master swapped and instance created. The optimizer commits transaction 1: pin connected or disconnected, pin connected or disconnected, instance created, pin connected or disconnected; transaction 2: pin connected or disconnected, pin connected or disconnected; transaction 3: master swapped, master swapped, pin connected or disconnected. How many observer calls does the database make?
problems.e: Per transaction, count the observers touched at least once: 3 + 1 + 2, total 6. Per-edit notification would have made 13 calls.

problems.q: A database batches notifications: at each commit, every observer subscribed to at least one edit kind in the transaction gets exactly one call carrying the list of edits. Observers: the parasitic estimator subscribes to master swapped, pin connected or disconnected and instance created; the density map subscribes to instance moved; the power analyzer subscribes to master swapped. The optimizer commits transaction 1: instance created, pin connected or disconnected; transaction 2: pin connected or disconnected, pin connected or disconnected, instance created, instance moved; transaction 3: instance created, master swapped; transaction 4: master swapped, instance moved. How many observer calls does the database make?
problems.e: Per transaction, count the observers touched at least once: 1 + 2 + 2 + 3, total 8. Per-edit notification would have made 12 calls.

label: Incremental computation and dependency graphs
lesson:
# Incremental computation and dependency graphs

Every EDA tool caches derived results: parasitics computed from wires, delays from parasitics, arrivals from delays, slacks from arrivals. When the design changes, recomputing everything is too slow, and recomputing too little gives wrong answers. A dependency graph makes the cache honest. Each derived result is a node, each edge says which input it was computed from, and an edit tells the tool exactly which cached values may now be stale. This structure sits underneath incremental timing, incremental legalization and incremental builds alike.

## Invalidation follows forward edges

Draw an edge $u \to v$ whenever result $v$ is computed from $u$. The graph is acyclic, because no result can depend on itself, so it has a topological order. When an edit modifies node $u$, every node reachable from $u$ along edges may be stale, and no other node can be: its inputs are untouched. The invalid set is therefore the forward reachable set of the edited nodes, found by one depth-first or breadth-first search.

Example: edges $A \to B$, $A \to C$, $B \to D$, $C \to D$, $D \to E$ and $F \to E$. An edit to $B$ invalidates $D$ and $E$, two results; $A$, $C$ and $F$ keep their cached values. With several edits, the invalid set is the union of their reachable sets, so a result reachable from two edits is invalidated once, not twice.

## A query needs only its dirty ancestors

Invalidation is cheap; recomputation is the expensive part, and a lazy tool postpones it until someone asks. A query for node $q$ must bring $q$ up to date, and that requires every input of $q$ to be valid first, recursively. So the work for one query is the set of dirty nodes that are $q$ itself or ancestors of $q$. Dirty nodes elsewhere stay dirty.

Continuing the example, edit $B$ and then query $D$. The dirty set is $\{D, E\}$. The ancestors of $D$ are $A$, $B$ and $C$, all clean, so only $D$ is recomputed: one evaluation, although two results are dirty. A query for $E$ would recompute $D$ and then $E$. This is why a timer asked for the slack of one endpoint touches only that endpoint's fanin cone.

## Recompute in levels

When everything dirty must be refreshed, the topological order says what may run together. Give each dirty node a level: one more than the highest level among its dirty inputs, and 1 if all its inputs are clean. Nodes on the same level do not depend on one another, so a parallel engine can recompute a whole level at once, and the number of rounds equals the deepest level.

Example: edit $A$ in the graph above. Dirty nodes are $B$, $C$, $D$ and $E$. $B$ and $C$ have only the clean input $A$, so both are level 1. $D$ depends on $B$ and $C$, so level 2. $E$ depends on $D$ and the clean $F$, so level 3. Three rounds, the longest dirty path, however many workers there are. Long dependency chains limit incremental parallelism just as they limit full recomputation.

## Going deeper

Acar, "Self-Adjusting Computation" (PhD thesis, Carnegie Mellon, 2005); the Salsa and Adapton papers on demand-driven incremental computation; the OpenSTA source for how a timer tracks invalid arrivals.

problems.q: A tool caches derived results in a dependency graph whose edges run from an input to a result computed from it: R→C, H→C, L→F, L→E, H→E, L→J, R→H, E→G, R→L. An edit directly modifies L. How many results, not counting the edited node itself, must be marked invalid?
problems.e: Invalidation follows edges forward: every result reachable from L may now be stale. Those are E, F, G, J, 4 results.

label: Dirty flags and lazy invalidation
lesson:
# Dirty flags and lazy invalidation

A dirty flag is one bit per cached result that says "my inputs changed since I was computed." Setting flags is cheap, recomputing is not, and the gap between the two is where incremental tools win. An eager tool recomputes after every edit; a lazy one marks results dirty and recomputes only when a value is read. Combined with early cutoff, which stops propagation when a recomputed value comes out unchanged, dirty flags let an optimizer make thousands of edits between expensive queries.

## Eager recomputation after every edit

In the eager scheme, each edit immediately recomputes every result downstream of the edited node. The cost of a sequence of edits is the sum of the downstream set sizes, edit by edit, and results shared by several edits are paid for every time.

Example: edges $A \to C$, $B \to C$, $C \to D$, $D \to E$. A script edits $A$ and then $B$. Editing $A$ recomputes $C$, $D$ and $E$: three evaluations. Editing $B$ recomputes $C$, $D$ and $E$ again: three more. Total six. If the script makes $k$ edits that all feed the same cone of size $m$, eager evaluation costs $km$. Eager evaluation is simple and always leaves values valid, which is why it survives in small tools, but it scales badly when an optimizer makes many edits per query.

## Mark dirty, recompute on demand

In the lazy scheme, an edit walks forward and sets the dirty flag of every downstream result, stopping at results already dirty, since their descendants were flagged earlier. Nothing is recomputed until a read. A read of a dirty result first refreshes its dirty inputs, recursively, then clears the flag. If every result is eventually read once, each dirty result is recomputed exactly once.

For the same example, edits to $A$ and $B$ flag $C$, $D$ and $E$, the union of the two downstream sets. One query pass recomputes three results instead of six. In general lazy cost is the size of the union, eager cost the sum of the parts, and the saving grows with the overlap between edits. The price is that every read must check a flag, and code that reads cached fields directly, bypassing the check, silently returns stale data.

## Early cutoff on unchanged values

Dirty means "might have changed," not "has changed." When a result is recomputed and its new value equals the old one, its dependents see identical inputs and need no work. Early cutoff exploits this: re-evaluate a node only if at least one of its inputs actually changed value.

Example: edges $A \to B$, $B \to C$, $C \to D$, $A \to E$. An edit changes $A$, so $B$ and $E$ are re-evaluated. Suppose $B$ comes out unchanged, which happens in timing when the arrival at a pin is set by another, slower fanin. Then $C$ and $D$ are not re-evaluated, so only $B$ and $E$ are: two evaluations instead of four. A node reachable by another path that avoids $B$ is still re-evaluated. Cutoff needs a cheap equality test, which is one reason timers compare arrivals with a small tolerance rather than recomputing bit-exact values.

## Going deeper

Mokhov, Mitchell and Peyton Jones, "Build Systems à la Carte" (ICFP 2018), for dirty bits and early cutoff in build systems; the OpenSTA source for how it marks and refreshes invalid arrivals.

label: Incremental STA inside a tool
lesson:
# Incremental STA inside a tool

Inside an optimizer, a static timer is not a batch program that reads files and prints a report. It is a service living in the same process as the database, answering slack queries while the resizer, placer and router edit the netlist under it. Turning the timing-graph mathematics of incremental update into working software takes three pieces of infrastructure: a way to hear about edits, a way to record and refresh what they invalidate, and an understanding of which edits and queries are cheap.

## Edits reach the timer through callbacks

Tools that share one database learn about each other's edits through observers. The timer registers callbacks with the database; when an engine creates or deletes an instance, swaps its master, connects or disconnects a pin, or moves a cell, the database calls the timer before or after the change. The callback does not recompute timing. It updates the timer's own graph to match the database, adding or removing vertices and arcs, and it marks what is now stale: the delays of the affected arcs, the arrivals downstream and the required times upstream.

Callbacks must be fast, because a placement pass may produce tens of thousands of them. Recording "these pins are invalid" is constant work per edit; recomputing on each callback would multiply the cost of every edit by the size of a cone. Edits that change no electrical fact, such as renaming a net, should not invalidate anything.

## Invalidate, then propagate in level order

Invalidation splits into two directions. An arc change at $u \to v$ can change arrivals at $v$ and in its fanout cone, and required times at $u$ and in its fanin cone. A timer keeps separate invalid sets for the two, plus a set of arcs whose delays must be recalculated.

When a query arrives, the timer recomputes delays for invalid arcs, then processes invalid arrivals in increasing level order, so that every fanin is final before a pin's max is taken; required times are processed in decreasing level order. Two refinements matter. First, demand: a query for one endpoint's slack refreshes only its fanin cone and its own required time. Second, early termination: if a pin's new arrival equals its old one, its fanout need not be visited. OpenSTA implements this levelized lazy scheme; OpenTimer instead builds a task graph for the invalid region and runs it on a parallel task scheduler.

## What makes an incremental update expensive

Incrementality pays only when the changed region is small and the questions are local. Three patterns break it. A constraint edit, such as a new clock period or a changed input delay, alters required times at many endpoints, so the backward update can cover most of the design. A global query after every edit, such as asking for worst negative slack following each buffer insertion, forces a near-global refresh each time, so 10,000 edits cost 10,000 global updates. And structural edits that lengthen paths, such as inserting a buffer, can raise the levels of downstream pins, so level bookkeeping must itself be updated incrementally.

Good optimizer code batches edits, asks local questions (the slack of the endpoints it touched), and saves global summaries for checkpoints. A useful mental model: the cost of an update is the size of the region a query forces valid, not the size of the edit.

## Going deeper

The OpenSTA source and its documentation on network edits and incremental timing; Huang and Wong, "OpenTimer: A High-Performance Timing Analysis Tool" (ICCAD 2015) and the later OpenTimer 2 paper on task-based incremental timing.

problems.q:
A resizer swaps a NAND2_X1 for a NAND2_X4 through the database API. How does an incremental timer embedded in the same process learn about the change?

A) It re-times the full design on a timer every second

B) It rereads the netlist file at the next report

C) The resizer must call a full update_timing after every swap

D) A database callback fires and the timer marks the affected pins invalid
problems.a: A database callback fires and the timer marks the affected pins invalid
problems.e: Tools sharing one database register observers; the swap notifies the timer, which records what is now stale instead of recomputing on the spot.

problems.q:
A placer moves 50,000 cells in one detailed-placement pass, each move reported by a callback. What is the sensible way for the timer to respond?

A) Ignore moves, since placement never changes delay

B) Run a full incremental update after each of the 50,000 moves

C) Recompute only the slack of the moved cells' output pins

D) Accumulate invalidations and recompute once at the next timing query
problems.a: Accumulate invalidations and recompute once at the next timing query
problems.e: Moves change wire parasitics and so delays. Batching the invalidations until a query amortizes the update across all moves.

problems.q:
A placer moves 50,000 cells in one detailed-placement pass, each move reported by a callback. What is the sensible way for the timer to respond?

A) Recompute only the slack of the moved cells' output pins

B) Accumulate invalidations and recompute once at the next timing query

C) Ignore moves, since placement never changes delay

D) Run a full incremental update after each of the 50,000 moves
problems.a: Accumulate invalidations and recompute once at the next timing query
problems.e: Moves change wire parasitics and so delays. Batching the invalidations until a query amortizes the update across all moves.

problems.q:
Why does an incremental timer track required times separately from arrival times when invalidating?

A) Arrivals depend on the fanin cone, required times on the fanout cone, so an arc edit invalidates them in opposite directions

B) Both flow forward, so one set of flags would duplicate the other

C) Required times never change after the SDC is read

D) Arrival times are stored in the database and required times are not
problems.a: Arrivals depend on the fanin cone, required times on the fanout cone, so an arc edit invalidates them in opposite directions
problems.e: An arc change affects arrivals at and after its head, and required times at and before its tail, so the two sets of flags cover different pins.

problems.q:
After a batch of edits, an incremental timer has a set of pins with invalid arrival times. In what order must it recompute them?

A) In any order, because each arrival is computed independently

B) In increasing level order, so every fanin is final before a pin is evaluated

C) In the order the edits arrived

D) In decreasing level order from the endpoints
problems.a: In increasing level order, so every fanin is final before a pin is evaluated
problems.e: An arrival is a max over fanin arrivals plus delays, so it can only be computed once its fanins are up to date; levelized order guarantees that.

problems.q:
A query asks for the slack of one endpoint after an edit. Which values must be brought up to date for that answer?

A) The required times of every startpoint in its fanin cone

B) Only the arrival at the endpoint itself

C) The invalid arrivals in its fanin cone and its own required time

D) Every invalid arrival and required time in the design
problems.a: The invalid arrivals in its fanin cone and its own required time
problems.e: Slack at an endpoint is its required minus its arrival. The arrival depends on the fanin cone; the endpoint's required time comes from its clock and constraints.

problems.q:
OpenTimer differs from a classic levelized incremental update in how it executes the recomputation. What does it use?

A) A SAT solver to find which arcs changed

B) Monte Carlo sampling of the affected paths

C) A task graph of the affected work, run in parallel by a work-stealing scheduler

D) A complete re-timing on a GPU after every edit
problems.a: A task graph of the affected work, run in parallel by a work-stealing scheduler
problems.e: OpenTimer builds a task dependency graph for the invalid region and executes it with a parallel task scheduler, so independent parts update concurrently.

problems.q:
Which edit is typically the most expensive for an incremental timer to absorb?

A) Inserting one buffer on a high-fanout net

B) Moving one cell by a few sites

C) Changing a clock period in the constraints

D) Upsizing one cell on a critical path
problems.a: Changing a clock period in the constraints
problems.e: A clock change alters required times at every endpoint of that clock and therefore across most of the design, whereas a netlist edit has a local cone.

problems.q:
A buffer insertion adds a new instance and splits a net. What must happen to the timing graph's levels?

A) Levels never change after the first levelization

B) Every level in the design must be renumbered from scratch

C) Only the buffer's input pin needs a level

D) The new pins need levels, and pins downstream may need their levels raised
problems.a: The new pins need levels, and pins downstream may need their levels raised
problems.e: The buffer lengthens the path, so the levels of its fanout may rise. Timers update levels incrementally for the affected region rather than relevelizing everything.

label: Incremental legalization
prereqs: Rows, sites and the placement region
lesson:
# Incremental legalization

After global placement, a legalizer snaps every cell to a row and a site without overlap. During optimization, though, the design changes a little at a time: a resizer widens a cell, a buffer is inserted, a cell is moved. Re-legalizing the whole design for each change would scramble a carefully optimized placement and take far too long. Incremental legalization repairs only the neighbourhood of the change, moving as few cells as possible by as little as possible, which keeps timing and wirelength close to what the optimizer saw.

## Push-right shifting in a row

The simplest incremental repair works inside one row. Cells are kept sorted by x, each with a left edge $x_i$ and width $w_i$ in site units. When cell $k$ grows by $g$ sites with its left edge fixed, its right edge moves from $x_k + w_k$ to $x_k + w_k + g$. Walk right: each later cell must start at or after the right edge of its left neighbour, so its new position is $x'_i = \max(x_i,\ x'_{i-1} + w_{i-1})$. The walk stops changing anything at the first cell whose gap absorbs the push.

Example: cells at $x = 0$ (width 4), $x = 4$ (width 3), $x = 9$ (width 2) and $x = 11$ (width 5). Widen the first by 4. It now ends at 8, so the second moves to 8 and ends at 11. The third, at 9, must move to 11 and ends at 13. The fourth, at 11, moves to 13. Three cells move.

## Where a pushed cell lands

Each pushed cell lands exactly against its left neighbour, because the rule moves it by the least amount that removes the overlap. So positions in a pushed run are a running sum: the first pushed cell starts at the new right edge of the edited cell, and every following pushed cell starts at the right edge of the one before it, until a gap at least as large as the remaining push appears.

In the example, the pushed run is 8, 11, 13: the second cell at 8, the third at $8 + 3 = 11$, the fourth at $11 + 2 = 13$. Gaps before the edit were 0 between the first two cells, 2 between the second and third, and 0 between the third and fourth, so the push of 4 shrank to 2 after the first gap and stayed 2. A useful check: the shift of each pushed cell equals the push it received minus the gap in front of it.

## Total displacement and when to stop

The cost of an incremental repair is usually measured as total displacement, the sum of $|x'_i - x_i|$ over moved cells, because every moved cell perturbs its nets and the timing the optimizer just evaluated. In the example the shifts are 4, 2 and 2, a total of 8 sites.

Pushing in one direction is cheap but not minimal: a run might be better split, with some cells moving left into earlier gaps, which is what a dynamic-programming legalizer such as Abacus does when it re-solves the cluster positions that minimize quadratic displacement. A push can also run off the end of the row, and then cells must move to a neighbouring row. Production legalizers, such as OpenROAD's dpl, therefore search for nearby legal sites within a window and fall back to wider repairs only when a window has no room. The engineering rule is to bound the region touched, so the update stays local and the placement keeps its quality.

## Going deeper

Spindler, Schlichtmann and Johannes, "Abacus: Fast Legalization of Standard Cell Circuits with Minimal Movement" (ISPD 2008); the OpenROAD documentation for dpl (detailed placement).

label: Content-addressed result caching
prereqs: Expected value of a random variable
lesson:
# Content-addressed result caching

Flows recompute the same things over and over: a regression reruns unchanged designs, a parameter sweep shares its synthesis step, a developer reruns placement after editing only a report script. A result cache stores each step's output under a key computed from its inputs, so an identical invocation is answered by a lookup. The idea is the same one build systems use for object files. It is worth doing only when lookups are cheap relative to the computation, and correct only when the key covers every input that affects the output.

## Expected time with a cache

Let a lookup cost $L$ (hashing the inputs and probing the store), the computation cost $C$, and the hit rate be $h$. Every invocation pays the lookup; only misses pay the computation. The expected time is
$$E[T] = L + (1 - h)\,C.$$
Writing the result back into the store on a miss adds a little more, which we ignore here.

Example: an extraction step takes $C = 300$ s, the lookup costs $L = 12$ s and the hit rate is 75%. Then $E[T] = 12 + 0.25 \times 300 = 87$ s, against 300 s without a cache. The expectation is a linearity-of-expectation statement over many invocations; any single call takes either 12 s or 312 s. Large flows care about the expectation because they run thousands of steps.

## The break-even hit rate

A cache can lose. A miss costs $L + C$, more than the uncached $C$, so the cache helps on average only when
$$L + (1 - h)\,C < C \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h > \frac{L}{C}.$$
Example: hashing a large netlist and probing remote storage costs $L = 20$ s, and the step runs in $C = 160$ s. The break-even hit rate is $20/160 = 12.5\%$. Above it the cache saves time; below it, the cache is overhead.

The ratio $L/C$ explains where caching belongs. Long steps (synthesis, global routing, extraction) have tiny break-even rates and are excellent candidates. Short steps whose inputs are large (a quick report over a full database) may never pay back the cost of hashing their inputs. Cheap keys help: hashing file contents once and reusing the digest is far faster than rehashing on every lookup.

## Keys must hash every input

A content-addressed cache names a result by a hash of everything that determines it: the input files, the step's parameters, the random seed, and the version of the tool binary. Identical keys must mean identical outputs. If any determining input is missing from the key, two different computations share a key and the cache returns a wrong result, silently, which is far worse than a slow run.

Example: runs arrive with (netlist, SDC, tool version, seed) equal to (1, 1, 1, 2), (1, 1, 2, 2), (1, 1, 1, 2), (2, 1, 1, 1). The first, second and fourth keys are new and miss; the third repeats the first and hits, one hit. A key that omitted the tool version would also report the second run as a hit and hand back a result from a different build. Environment variables, PDK files and hidden defaults are the usual omissions. Deterministic tools are a prerequisite: if the same inputs can give different outputs, a cache cannot be trusted at all.

## Going deeper

Mokhov, Mitchell and Peyton Jones, "Build Systems à la Carte" (ICFP 2018), on cloud build caches and constructive traces; the Bazel documentation on remote caching.

label: Amdahl's law and parallel speedup
lesson:
# Amdahl's law and parallel speedup

EDA runs are long, and machines have many cores, so every engine author is asked how much faster the tool gets with more threads. Amdahl's law gives the first answer: the part of the run that stays serial, such as reading the database, building data structures or writing results, caps the speedup no matter how many threads are added. Knowing the law tells a tool designer where to spend effort: shrinking the serial fraction often matters more than parallelizing the kernel further.

## Speedup with a serial fraction

Split a single-threaded run of time $T_1$ into a serial fraction $s$ and a parallel fraction $1 - s$. On $p$ threads, ideally only the parallel part shrinks:
$$T_p = T_1\left(s + \frac{1 - s}{p}\right), \qquad S(p) = \frac{T_1}{T_p} = \frac{1}{s + (1 - s)/p}.$$
Example: a global-placement run is 10% serial. On 16 threads, $S = 1/(0.1 + 0.9/16) = 1/0.15625 = 6.4$. Sixteen threads give a speedup of 6.4, and the efficiency $S/p$ is only 40%. The formula is optimistic, since it ignores synchronization, memory bandwidth and load imbalance, so measured speedups are usually lower still.

## The ceiling of one over s

As $p \to \infty$ the parallel term $(1 - s)/p$ goes to zero and
$$\lim_{p \to \infty} S(p) = \frac{1}{s}.$$
Example: a single-threaded detailed-routing run takes 400 s, of which 20 s is serial: $s = 20/400 = 0.05$, so no machine can make it more than 20 times faster. With 32 threads the run reaches $1/(0.05 + 0.95/32) \approx 12.55$, already most of the way to the ceiling, and doubling to 64 threads gives only about 15.42.

The ceiling explains why engine teams attack serial phases: parsing Liberty and LEF/DEF in parallel, building the timing graph concurrently, overlapping file output with computation. Halving the serial fraction doubles the ceiling, which no number of extra cores can do.

## Serial fraction from a target speedup

Turn the law around to set a budget. If a product needs speedup $S$ on $p$ threads, solve $S = 1/(s + (1 - s)/p)$ for $s$:
$$s = \frac{p/S - 1}{p - 1}.$$
Example: a router must run 12 times faster on 16 threads. Then $s = (16/12 - 1)/15 = 0.3333/15 \approx 0.0222$: at most about 2.22% of the single-threaded run may be serial. That number becomes an engineering requirement for every phase outside the parallel kernel.

Amdahl assumes a fixed problem. Gustafson's view, that bigger machines are used for bigger designs, gives a gentler picture when the parallel work grows with the design while the serial setup does not. Both views agree that the serial part has to be measured, not guessed, before parallel work is planned.

## Going deeper

Amdahl, "Validity of the Single Processor Approach to Achieving Large Scale Computing Capabilities" (AFIPS 1967); Gustafson, "Reevaluating Amdahl's Law" (CACM 1988); Herlihy and Shavit, "The Art of Multiprocessor Programming", chapter 1.

label: Thread pools and partitioned work
lesson:
# Thread pools and partitioned work

Parallel EDA engines rarely spawn a thread per task. They split the work into pieces (regions for routing, nets for extraction, partitions for placement) and feed them to a fixed pool of worker threads. How the pieces are ordered and assigned decides how close the run gets to the ideal: with uneven pieces, one long task can leave the other workers idle at the end. The makespan, the time until the last worker finishes, is the number to reason about.

## Greedy list scheduling

In list scheduling, tasks wait in a queue and each idle worker takes the next one. Equivalently, each task in order goes to the worker that becomes free first. The makespan is the largest worker load.

Example: tasks of 5, 3, 8, 2, 4 and 6 ms on 2 workers, ties going to the lower-numbered worker. Worker 1 takes 5 and worker 2 takes 3. Worker 2 is free first (at 3), so it takes 8 and is busy until 11. Worker 1 (at 5) takes 2, then at 7 takes 4, ending at 11. Both are at 11; the tie goes to worker 1, which takes 6 and finishes at 17. Makespan: 17 ms, while worker 2 sits idle from 11. Greedy scheduling is never worse than twice the optimum, but the order of the queue matters.

## Longest task first

Sorting the queue from longest to shortest before scheduling, the LPT rule, avoids leaving a long task for the end, when it cannot be balanced against anything. For the same tasks, the order is 8, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2. Worker 1 takes 8, worker 2 takes 6. Worker 2 is free first and takes 5 (ending at 11), worker 1 at 8 takes 4 (12), worker 2 at 11 takes 3 (14), worker 1 at 12 takes 2 (14). Makespan: 14 ms instead of 17.

LPT is guaranteed to be within a factor $4/3 - 1/(3p)$ of optimal. Engines apply the same idea by estimating task cost in advance: routing regions by pin count, nets by fanout. When costs cannot be predicted, smaller pieces and work stealing (an idle worker takes queued work from a busy one) keep the imbalance small at the end.

## Lower bounds on makespan

No schedule on $p$ workers can finish before
$$T^* \ge \max\left(\frac{\sum_i t_i}{p},\ \max_i t_i\right):$$
the total work must be shared among $p$ workers, and the longest task runs on one worker whatever happens. With dependencies between tasks, the longest dependency chain, the critical path, is a further bound.

In the example the total is 28 ms, so 2 workers need at least 14 ms, and the longest task is 8 ms. The bound is 14 ms, which LPT achieves, so LPT is optimal here. Comparing a schedule with this bound tells an engineer whether to fix the scheduler (a large gap) or to split the longest task (when $\max_i t_i$ dominates, as with one giant net or one congested region). A single 8 ms task on 8 workers with 16 ms total work gives a bound of 8 ms, not 2.

## Going deeper

Graham, "Bounds on Multiprocessing Timing Anomalies" (SIAM J. Applied Mathematics, 1969); the Taskflow documentation, used by OpenTimer, for task-graph scheduling with work stealing.

label: Deterministic parallelism
lesson:
# Deterministic parallelism

A deterministic engine gives bit-identical results for identical inputs, every run. Parallelism threatens this even without bugs: threads finish in different orders, floating-point sums depend on order, and shared random generators hand out numbers by timing. EDA teams insist on determinism because regression testing, bug reproduction, result caching and QoR comparison all assume it. A wirelength that drifts by 0.01% between identical runs hides real 0.01% regressions and makes field bugs impossible to reproduce.

## Floating-point sums depend on order

Floating-point addition rounds after every operation, so it is not associative: $(a + b) + c$ can differ from $a + (b + c)$. In decimal arithmetic rounded to 4 significant digits, $(1000 + 0.4) + 0.4$ rounds to 1000 at each step, while $1000 + (0.4 + 0.4) = 1000 + 0.8 = 1000.8$, which rounds to 1001. Double precision behaves the same way in its last bits.

A parallel reduction (the total wirelength, the density penalty, a gradient sum) combines partial sums in whatever order threads finish. Run twice, it can produce totals that differ in the last digits, with no race and no bug. In an iterative optimizer that difference does not stay small: it flips a comparison, a different move is accepted, and the final placements diverge. So bitwise reproducibility, not just "close enough," is the usual requirement.

## Fixed partitions and ordered merges

The cure is to make every rounding step and every merge independent of timing. Three techniques cover most cases. First, partition statically: split the index range into fixed chunks and compute a partial result per chunk. Second, merge in a fixed order: combine chunk results by chunk index, never as they arrive, and write per-item results into slots keyed by item index rather than appending to a shared list. Third, key randomness to work, not to threads: derive each item's random stream from the run seed and the item index, so the same item sees the same numbers whatever thread runs it.

If the chunking is chosen independently of the thread count, the result is also identical on 4 threads and on 32. A mutex is not a fix: it removes a race, but the order in which threads take the lock still varies, so an order-dependent result still varies.

## Deterministic tie-breaking and thread-count independence

Even single-threaded code hides nondeterminism. Iterating a hash map whose order depends on insertion history or a randomized hash seed, sorting by pointer address, reading uninitialized memory, or picking "the first" of equal-cost candidates from an unordered container all make results vary between runs. The rule is to break every tie with a stable key, such as an instance index or a name, and to sort by persistent ids, never by addresses.

The payoff is practical. A bug found on a 64-core server reproduces on a laptop. A regression that changes QoR on a commit touching only comments points to a determinism bug, not noise. Differential tests can demand identical outputs. Engines such as OpenROAD's tools aim to give the same result for the same inputs and seed, and treat any violation as a defect. The cost is usually a few percent of speed, from static partitioning and ordered merges.

## Going deeper

Goldberg, "What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic" (ACM Computing Surveys, 1991); Demmel and Nguyen, "Fast Reproducible Floating-Point Summation" (ARITH 2013); Bocchino et al., "Parallel Programming Must Be Deterministic by Default" (HotPar 2009).

C) Floating-point addition is not associative, and the reduction order differed

problems.e: With dynamic scheduling, partial sums are combined in whatever order threads finish. Rounding depends on order, so the last digits move even with no race.

A team wants results to be identical whether a job runs on 4 threads or 32. Which design achieves that?

A) Seed each thread's random generator with its thread ID

B) Let threads steal work and merge whichever partial result arrives first

C) Partition the work into a fixed number of chunks independent of the thread count and reduce chunks in order

D) Give each thread an equal share of the work, sized by the thread count
problems.a: Partition the work into a fixed number of chunks independent of the thread count and reduce chunks in order
problems.e: If the chunking depends on the thread count, the rounding and the random streams change with it. Fixed chunks with fixed seeds and ordered reduction make the thread count a pure performance knob.

problems.q:
A router processes nets in parallel and each thread appends its finished nets to a shared output list. The list order varies from run to run. What is the standard fix?

A) Give each work item an index and merge results in index order

B) Protect the list with a mutex

C) Run the router with a single thread in production

D) Sort threads by their operating-system ID
problems.a: Give each work item an index and merge results in index order
problems.e: A mutex removes the race but not the order dependence. Writing results to slots keyed by item index, then merging in that order, gives the same output whatever the timing.

problems.q:
A tool sorts instances by pointer address to get a stable order for a heuristic. Results differ between runs. Why?

A) Allocation addresses differ from run to run, so the order changes

B) Pointer comparison is undefined for any two objects

C) Pointers are always sorted in allocation order

D) Sorting is not stable for equal keys
problems.a: Allocation addresses differ from run to run, so the order changes
problems.e: Address layout depends on the allocator, address-space randomization and earlier allocations. Use a persistent ID or name as the key.

problems.q:
A regression flags a 0.1% wirelength change on a commit that only touched comments. The engine is supposedly deterministic. What should the team suspect first?

A) The test design was changed by the commit

B) The compiler optimized the comments

C) A hidden source of nondeterminism such as unordered iteration, timing-dependent merging or uninitialized memory

D) Wirelength always varies by 0.1% between runs
problems.a: A hidden source of nondeterminism such as unordered iteration, timing-dependent merging or uninitialized memory
problems.e: Deterministic engines should produce bit-identical results from identical inputs. A change without a cause is a determinism bug, and it would hide real regressions.

problems.q:
A regression flags a 0.1% wirelength change on a commit that only touched comments. The engine is supposedly deterministic. What should the team suspect first?

A) A hidden source of nondeterminism such as unordered iteration, timing-dependent merging or uninitialized memory

B) The test design was changed by the commit

C) Wirelength always varies by 0.1% between runs

D) The compiler optimized the comments
problems.a: A hidden source of nondeterminism such as unordered iteration, timing-dependent merging or uninitialized memory
problems.e: Deterministic engines should produce bit-identical results from identical inputs. A change without a cause is a determinism bug, and it would hide real regressions.

label: Conflict-free parallel batches
lesson:
# Conflict-free parallel batches

Many EDA engines work on a grid of regions: detailed routers route tiles, legalizers repair windows, DRC engines check windows with halos. Neighbouring regions can touch the same wires or cells, so processing them simultaneously would race. Locks per object are slow and nondeterministic. A cleaner scheme colors the regions so that no two neighbours share a color, then processes one color at a time: inside a color, regions are independent and run in parallel with no locks at all.

## Coloring tiles so batches never conflict

Model each tile as a vertex and join two tiles that may conflict; a batch must be an independent set, and a coloring partitions the tiles into batches. For a rectangular grid where tiles conflict when they share an edge or a corner, the coloring by $(r \bmod 2,\ c \bmod 2)$ works: two tiles with the same color differ by at least 2 in row or column, so they never touch. Four colors are also necessary, since any 2 × 2 block contains four mutually adjacent tiles.

Example: a 5 × 7 grid. Rows 0, 2 and 4 are even (3 rows); columns 0, 2, 4 and 6 are even (4 columns). The even-even batch has $3 \times 4 = 12$ tiles. The other batches have $3 \times 3 = 9$, $2 \times 4 = 8$ and $2 \times 3 = 6$, which sum to the 35 tiles. If only edge-sharing tiles conflicted, a checkerboard with two colors would do.

## Rounds with a fixed worker count

Batches run one after another, separated by a barrier, because a tile in a later batch may touch tiles of the current one. Inside a batch of $n_k$ tiles, $p$ workers handle $p$ tiles per round, so the batch takes $\lceil n_k / p \rceil$ rounds, and the whole grid takes
$$R = \sum_{k} \left\lceil \frac{n_k}{p} \right\rceil.$$
For the 5 × 7 grid with $p = 4$: $\lceil 12/4 \rceil + \lceil 9/4 \rceil + \lceil 8/4 \rceil + \lceil 6/4 \rceil = 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 = 10$ rounds. The ceilings are the cost of the barriers: a batch of 9 tiles leaves three workers idle in its last round. Engines reduce that waste with more tiles than workers, so the last partial round is a small part of each batch, or by letting idle workers begin the next batch's tiles that do not touch unfinished ones.

## Speedup of a batched schedule

If every tile takes the same time $t$, the serial run takes $nt$ for $n$ tiles and the batched run takes $Rt$, so the speedup is $n/R$, at most $p$. For the example, $35/10 = 3.5$ on 4 workers: the partial final rounds cost 12.5%.

The scheme has two further virtues. It is deterministic, because which tiles run together and in what batch order is fixed by the coloring, not by timing, so the results do not depend on thread scheduling. And it needs no locks inside a batch. The trade-off is idle time at barriers and sensitivity to uneven tiles: one congested tile makes its whole batch wait. Real routers therefore size tiles to balance work and process batches with a task pool, but keep the coloring that makes concurrent tiles independent.

## Going deeper

The TritonRoute papers on parallel detailed routing (Kahng, Wang and Xu); Jones and Plassmann, "A Parallel Graph Coloring Heuristic" (SIAM J. Scientific Computing, 1993).

problems.q: A detailed router divides the die into a 3 × 6 grid of tiles (3 rows, 6 columns). Two tiles that share an edge or a corner may touch the same wires, so they must never be routed at the same time. The tiles are colored by (row mod 2, column mod 2), giving four batches; batches run one after another, and inside a batch any tiles may run together. Rows and columns are numbered from 0. How many tiles are in the batch with even row and even column?
problems.e: Even rows: ceil(3/2) = 2. Even columns: ceil(6/2) = 3. The batch holds 2 × 3 = 6 tiles, and no two of them touch, since any two differ by at least two in row or in column.

problems.e: Even rows: ceil(5/2) = 3. Even columns: ceil(7/2) = 4. The batch holds 3 × 4 = 12 tiles, and no two of them touch, since any two differ by at least two in row or in column.

With 2 worker threads, each routing one tile per round, how many rounds does the whole grid take?

The tiles are colored by (row mod 2, column mod 2), giving four batches; batches run one after another, and inside a batch any tiles may run together. Every tile takes 40 ms. With 5 worker threads, each routing one tile per round, what is the speedup over routing all tiles on one thread? Round to 2 decimal places.

problems.e: Serially: 24 tiles × 30 ms = 720 ms. Batched: 8 rounds (6 tiles → 2 rounds, 6 tiles → 2 rounds, 6 tiles → 2 rounds, 6 tiles → 2 rounds) × 30 ms = 240 ms. Speedup = 3, below 3 because rounds at the end of each batch are only partly full.

label: Distributed runs, containers and the cloud
lesson:
# Distributed runs, containers and the cloud

A single flow run fits on one machine, but EDA work rarely comes as one run: regressions run dozens of designs, sweeps run hundreds of parameter sets, characterization runs thousands of independent simulations. Teams spread that work across clusters and clouds, which raises three problems a tool builder must solve: making every machine run the same software, sizing and paying for the fleet, and moving large design data to where the computation happens without breaking the IP boundary.

## Containers pin the tool environment

A container image packages a flow's user space: tool binaries such as Yosys, OpenROAD and KLayout, the libraries they link, the Python interpreter and its packages. Every host that runs the image sees the same versions, so a flow that passed in CI behaves the same on a laptop and on a cluster node. Containers share the host's Linux kernel; isolation comes from kernel namespaces, and resource limits from cgroups, which can cap a job's memory and CPU so that one runaway router does not take down the other jobs on the node.

Reproducibility depends on naming the image exactly. A mutable tag such as latest can be moved to a new build; pinning an image by its content digest names one immutable image. The PDK and design data are usually mounted into the container rather than baked in, which keeps images small and keeps proprietary data out of shared registries.

## Sizing a parameter sweep

For $J$ independent jobs of $t$ hours each on $M$ machines that run one job at a time, the jobs run in $\lceil J/M \rceil$ waves, so the wall-clock time is $\lceil J/M \rceil\, t$. Cost depends on billing. If machines are reserved for the whole sweep, you pay for $M \lceil J/M \rceil t$ machine-hours, idle ones in the last wave included. If an autoscaling pool bills only while a job runs, you pay for $J t$ machine-hours whatever $M$ is: the pool size changes the wall time, not the cost.

Example: 50 runs of 2 h on 8 machines take $\lceil 50/8 \rceil = 7$ waves, 14 h. Reserved at 1.5 credits per machine-hour, the cost is $8 \times 14 \times 1.5 = 168$ credits; billed per job, it is $50 \times 2 \times 1.5 = 150$ credits. Adding machines to 50 would cut the wall time to 2 h at the same per-job cost.

## Scheduling, storage and data locality

Independent jobs scale out almost perfectly; one tightly coupled run that shares a large in-memory database does not, because splitting it across machines turns memory accesses into network messages. So EDA distribution is mostly about many independent jobs, orchestrated as a graph of steps by a scheduler or workflow engine. Two engineering points dominate. Storage: hundreds of jobs reading a 30 GB database each at the same moment saturate a shared file system, so inputs are staged or cached near the compute. Restartability: if each step writes its outputs to durable storage keyed by its inputs, a failed sweep resumes from where it stopped, and cheap preemptible machines become usable for short jobs.

Cloud use also raises an architectural question that is not about price: foundry agreements and IP policy constrain where design and PDK data may live and who may access it, so tenancy, encryption and data residency are part of the design.

## Going deeper

The Linux kernel documentation on cgroups and namespaces; the OpenROAD-flow-scripts documentation on running the flow in Docker; Dean and Barroso, "The Tail at Scale" (CACM 2013), on large-fleet job behaviour.

A container image tag such as latest is used in a regression flow. Why is that risky?

A) The tag can point to a different image later, so the flow is not reproducible

B) Containers ignore tags at run time

C) Tags slow down image pulls

D) A tag forces the container to run as root
problems.a: The tag can point to a different image later, so the flow is not reproducible
problems.e: A mutable tag can be moved to a new build. Pinning an image by its content digest names exactly one image.

A container image tag such as latest is used in a regression flow. Why is that risky?

A) Tags slow down image pulls

B) Containers ignore tags at run time

C) A tag forces the container to run as root

D) The tag can point to a different image later, so the flow is not reproducible
problems.a: The tag can point to a different image later, so the flow is not reproducible
problems.e: A mutable tag can be moved to a new build. Pinning an image by its content digest names exactly one image.

problems.q:
A memory-hungry routing job is run inside a container with a cgroup memory limit of 64 GB and exceeds it. What happens?

A) The kernel kills the process in that cgroup when it cannot reclaim memory

B) Other containers on the host are killed first

C) The job swaps to the network file system

D) The container automatically grows its limit
problems.a: The kernel kills the process in that cgroup when it cannot reclaim memory
problems.e: cgroups enforce resource limits per group. Exceeding the memory limit triggers the out-of-memory killer for that group, which protects the other jobs on the host.

problems.q:
A sweep of 26 flow runs, 2.5 h each, runs on an autoscaling pool of up to 6 machines; a machine is billed only while it runs a job, at 1 credits per machine-hour. What does the sweep cost?

A) 65 credits

B) 12.5 credits

C) 75 credits

D) 130 credits
problems.a: 65 credits
problems.e: Billing follows the work, not the wall time: 26 jobs × 2.5 h × 1 = 65 credits. The pool size changes the 12.5 h wall time, not the cost.

problems.q:
A sweep of 79 flow runs, 1.5 h each, runs on an autoscaling pool of up to 9 machines; a machine is billed only while it runs a job, at 0.5 credits per machine-hour. What does the sweep cost?

A) 118.5 credits

B) 60.75 credits

C) 59.25 credits

D) 6.75 credits
problems.a: 59.25 credits
problems.e: Billing follows the work, not the wall time: 79 jobs × 1.5 h × 0.5 = 59.25 credits. The pool size changes the 13.5 h wall time, not the cost.

problems.q:
A sweep of 20 flow runs, 1.5 h each, runs on 27 cloud machines reserved for the whole sweep and billed at 2.25 credits per machine-hour, idle or not. Each machine runs one job at a time. What does the sweep cost?

A) 3.38 credits

B) 91.12 credits

C) 67.5 credits

D) 94.5 credits
problems.a: 91.12 credits
problems.e: The sweep takes ceil(20/27) = 1 waves, 1.5 h, and all 27 machines are billed for it: 27 × 1.5 × 2.25 = 91.12 credits. Releasing idle machines in the last wave would cost 67.5 credits.

problems.q:
Which job type benefits least from being split across many machines?

A) Characterizing each standard cell of a library separately

B) A sweep of 200 independent flow runs with different parameters

C) Running each regression design as its own job

D) One tightly coupled detailed-routing run that shares one in-memory database
problems.a: One tightly coupled detailed-routing run that shares one in-memory database
problems.e: Independent jobs scale out trivially. A single run that needs fast access to one shared database pays heavy communication costs when distributed.

problems.q:
A workflow orchestrator runs a flow as a graph of steps, each in its own container. A step fails halfway through a 100-step sweep. What property lets the sweep resume without redoing finished steps?

A) Steps share global variables in memory

B) The orchestrator restarts the sweep from the beginning

C) Every step runs in the same container

D) Each step writes its outputs to durable storage keyed by its inputs
problems.a: Each step writes its outputs to durable storage keyed by its inputs
problems.e: If finished outputs are recorded against their inputs, the orchestrator can skip completed steps and rerun only what failed or depends on it.

problems.q:
A cluster scheduler places 500 flow jobs. Each reads a 30 GB design database from shared storage. What is the likely bottleneck?

A) Shared storage bandwidth while all jobs load their inputs

B) CPU cycles spent parsing the scheduler's job file

C) The number of Linux users on the cluster

D) The container image size on each host
problems.a: Shared storage bandwidth while all jobs load their inputs
problems.e: Hundreds of jobs reading large inputs at once saturate the file system. Staging data locally or caching inputs near the compute relieves it.

label: License management and tool economics
prereqs: Distributed runs, containers and the cloud
lesson:
# License management and tool economics

Commercial EDA tools are licensed, usually as a pool of floating licenses served by a license server: a job checks out a license when it starts a licensed feature and checks it back in when done. Licenses, not machines, are often the scarce resource, since a site may have thousands of cores but a few dozen licenses of a signoff tool. Planning around licenses is ordinary scheduling arithmetic, and tool and flow builders influence it directly by deciding when a license is held.

## Licenses cap concurrency

If every job needs one license for its whole run and machines are plentiful, at most $L$ jobs run at once. $J$ jobs of $t$ hours then run in $\lceil J/L \rceil$ waves, and the batch takes $\lceil J/L \rceil\, t$ hours.

Example: 23 signoff timing runs of 3 h each with 5 licenses run in $\lceil 23/5 \rceil = 5$ waves: 15 h. Adding machines does nothing; adding a sixth license gives $\lceil 23/6 \rceil = 4$ waves, 12 h, and an eighth gives 3 waves, 9 h. This is why license counts are negotiated against schedules: a tape-out crunch that needs many signoff runs in parallel is a license question first. Open-source tools remove this constraint entirely, one of their practical attractions for regressions and sweeps, where thousands of runs would otherwise queue for licenses.

## License utilization

Over a batch, the licenses offer $L \times T_{wall}$ license-hours, and the jobs use $J t$. Utilization is
$$U = \frac{J t}{L\, \lceil J/L \rceil\, t} = \frac{J}{L \lceil J/L \rceil}.$$
In the example, $U = 23/(5 \times 5) = 92\%$: the last wave has only 3 jobs, so 2 licenses sit idle for 3 h. With 20 jobs, utilization would be 100%; with 21, a fifth wave holds a single job and $U = 21/25 = 84\%$.

Licenses are expensive, so sites measure utilization from license-server logs and fill idle capacity with lower-priority jobs. Queueing systems that are aware of licenses hold a job until its license is free, instead of starting it and letting it wait while it occupies a machine.

## Check in licenses early

A job holds a license for as long as it keeps it checked out, which is not necessarily its whole run. Suppose each job has a licensed phase of $b$ hours (the timing analysis itself) and then $c$ hours of unlicensed work (parsing reports, plotting, archiving). Holding the license until the end makes each job occupy it for $b + c$ hours: the batch takes $\lceil J/L \rceil (b + c)$. Checking in after the licensed phase lets the next job start: licensed phases run back to back in $\lceil J/L \rceil$ waves of $b$, and only the last wave's post-processing adds $c$, for $\lceil J/L \rceil\, b + c$.

Example: 12 jobs, 4 licenses, $b = 2$ h, $c = 1$ h. Holding: $3 \times 3 = 9$ h. Checking in: $3 \times 2 + 1 = 7$ h, saving 2 h with the same licenses. Flow builders apply the same idea by splitting jobs so that licensed steps do only licensed work.

## Going deeper

Vendor documentation for floating license servers (for example the FlexNet Publisher administration guide); Kahng et al., "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 1, on design cost and tools.

problems.q: Each of 6 jobs has a 5 h phase that needs the tool license, followed by a 1 h post-processing phase (report parsing and plotting) that does not. There are 3 licenses and plenty of machines. How many hours of wall-clock time are saved if each job checks its license back in when the licensed phase ends, instead of holding it until the job finishes?
problems.e: Holding: 2 waves × (5 + 1) h = 12 h. Checking in: the licensed phases run back to back in 2 waves of 5 h, and the last wave's post-processing adds 1 h, so 11 h. Saved: 1 h.

label: Regression testing and QoR tracking
lesson:
# Regression testing and QoR tracking

An EDA engine is never finished: every heuristic tweak, refactor or compiler upgrade can change results. Regression testing runs a fixed suite of designs through the tool on every change and compares quality of results (QoR), such as wirelength, worst slack, area, power and run time, against a stored baseline. The comparison must summarize many designs of very different sizes into one honest number, and the standard summary is the geometric mean of per-design ratios.

## Geometric mean of QoR ratios

For each design $i$, form the ratio $r_i = \text{new}_i / \text{old}_i$ of the candidate's metric to the baseline's. A ratio is scale free: a 1% change on a tiny design and on a huge one count equally, which raw differences would not. Summarize $n$ ratios by their geometric mean,
$$G = \left(\prod_{i=1}^{n} r_i\right)^{1/n} = \exp\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_i \ln r_i\right).$$
Example: routed wirelength on three designs goes 1000 → 900, 500 → 550 and 2000 → 2000. The ratios are 0.9, 1.1 and 1.0. Their product is 0.99, so $G = 0.99^{1/3} \approx 0.997$. Computing through logarithms avoids overflow and underflow when the suite has hundreds of designs.

## Reporting a percent change

A geometric-mean ratio is reported as a signed percentage, $(G - 1) \times 100$. For the example, $(0.9967 - 1) \times 100 \approx -0.33\%$: for a lower-is-better metric, a 0.33% improvement on average. Regression dashboards show this per metric and per commit, so a slow drift becomes visible long before any single design looks broken.

A summary must not hide outliers. A suite whose geometric mean improves by 1% while one design gets 15% worse has a real problem, so dashboards also show the per-design ratios and flag any design beyond a tolerance. Run time needs its own baseline machine and load, since it varies with the host, and metrics with mixed directions (lower is better for area, higher for slack margin) should be put on a common orientation before they are combined. Worst slack, which can be zero or negative, is better tracked as a difference than as a ratio.

## Why the geometric mean is symmetric

Compare the candidate with the baseline, or the baseline with the candidate: the conclusion should be the same. The geometric mean has exactly this property, because the geometric mean of the reciprocals is the reciprocal of the geometric mean:
$$\left(\prod_i \frac{1}{r_i}\right)^{1/n} = \frac{1}{G}.$$
For the example, baseline over candidate gives $1/0.9967 \approx 1.003$, the same 0.33% read from the other side.

The arithmetic mean fails this test. Take two designs, one twice as large and one half as large: ratios 2 and 0.5. Their arithmetic mean is 1.25, which says the candidate is 25% worse, and the arithmetic mean of the reciprocals, 0.5 and 2, is also 1.25, which says the baseline is 25% worse. Both cannot be true. The geometric mean gives 1 both ways, the correct reading of a gain and a loss that cancel in ratio terms.

## Going deeper

label: Seed noise and QoR significance
lesson:
# Seed noise and QoR significance

Placers and routers use randomness: initial positions, move orders, tie-breaking seeds. Change the seed and wirelength moves by a fraction of a percent with no change to the code. A regression that reports a 0.3% improvement is meaningless unless that number is compared with the seed-to-seed noise. Running several seeds before and after a change, and testing the paired differences, separates real improvements from luck. It is ordinary statistics, applied to the most common question in engine development.

## Paired differences across seeds

Run the old and the new build with the same seeds $1, \ldots, n$ and record the metric for each. Pairing removes the variation that the seed causes in both builds alike: a seed that happens to give a good placement gives a good one before and after. Analyze the per-seed differences $d_i = \text{after}_i - \text{before}_i$.

Example: routed wirelength in mm for four seeds, before → after: 500 → 497, 512 → 510, 488 → 487 and 505 → 498. The differences are $-3, -2, -1, -7$, and their mean is $\bar d = -13/4 = -3.25$ mm. A negative mean suggests that the change shortens wirelength. Whether -3.25 is real depends on how much the differences scatter. Pairing is legitimate only if the seed has the same meaning in both builds; if the change consumes random numbers in a different order, the pairing weakens and more seeds are needed.

## Seed-to-seed spread

The sample standard deviation of the differences measures their scatter:
$$s = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n - 1}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (d_i - \bar d)^2}.$$
Dividing by $n - 1$ rather than $n$ makes $s^2$ an unbiased estimate of the variance, which matters for the handful of seeds a regression can afford.

For the example, deviations from -3.25 are $0.25, 1.25, 2.25, -3.75$, with squares $0.0625, 1.5625, 5.0625, 14.0625$ summing to 20.75. Then $s = \sqrt{20.75/3} \approx 2.63$ mm. A spread of 2.63 mm against a mean of 3.25 mm says that individual seeds disagree considerably about the size of the effect. Knowing the typical spread of each metric on each design also sets sensible tolerances for the nightly regression: a band narrower than the seed noise would fail on noise alone.

## The paired t statistic

The paired t statistic divides the mean difference by its standard error:
$$t = \frac{\bar d}{s / \sqrt{n}}.$$
For the example, $t = -3.25 / (2.63/\sqrt 4) = -3.25 / 1.315 \approx -2.47$. Under the null hypothesis of no effect, $t$ follows a t distribution with $n - 1 = 3$ degrees of freedom, whose two-sided 5% critical value is about 3.18. Since $|t| = 2.47 < 3.18$, four seeds are not enough to call the improvement real at that level, though they hint at one.

More seeds shrink the standard error as $1/\sqrt n$, so quadrupling the seeds halves it. The practical lesson for tool builders: report QoR changes with their uncertainty, choose the number of seeds from the noise of each metric, and remember that testing many metrics on many designs at once produces false alarms unless the threshold accounts for it.

## Going deeper

Montgomery, "Design and Analysis of Experiments", chapter 2 on paired comparisons; Kahng and Mantik, "On Mismatches between Incremental Optimizers and Instance Perturbations in Physical Design Tools" (ICCAD 2000), on noise in placement results.

label: Build systems and incremental compilation
lesson:
# Build systems and incremental compilation

A modern EDA tool is millions of lines of C++ across thousands of files, and an engineer, or an agent in a harness loop, rebuilds it many times a day. A build system turns a source edit into the smallest set of recompilations and links that produce a correct binary. It does so with the same machinery as incremental computation: a dependency graph from sources and headers to object files to libraries, and invalidation that follows the graph. Header structure, more than compiler speed, decides how long an edit takes to test.

## Header changes recompile their dependents

In C++, each source file plus everything it includes is a translation unit, compiled to one object file. A translation unit depends on every header it includes directly or through other headers. Editing a header therefore invalidates every translation unit that reaches it in the include graph: a reverse reachability question.

Example: geom.h is included by db.h; net.h includes db.h; place.cpp includes net.h, route.cpp includes db.h, sta.cpp includes timer.h, and gui.cpp includes geom.h. An edit to geom.h recompiles place.cpp (through net.h and db.h), route.cpp (through db.h) and gui.cpp (directly): 3 translation units. An edit to timer.h recompiles only sta.cpp. Build tools such as Make with compiler-generated dependency files, or Ninja under CMake, record these edges after each compile, so the next build knows exactly which objects are stale.

## Parallel compile and the link step

Stale translation units are independent, so the build compiles them in parallel, up to $p$ jobs at once, and then links. If $k$ units each take $c$ seconds, the compile phase needs $\lceil k/p \rceil$ waves and the build takes $\lceil k/p \rceil\, c + L$, with $L$ the link time.

Example: an edit to a low-level header dirties 7 units of 20 s each, the build runs 4 jobs and the link takes 12 s: $\lceil 7/4 \rceil \times 20 + 12 = 52$ s. A one-line change in a .cpp file costs one compile and the link, 32 s. For small edits the link dominates, which is why large tools split into shared libraries or use fast linkers, and why compiler caches such as ccache, which return a stored object when the preprocessed input is unchanged, pay off when switching branches.

## Finding the most expensive header

The cost of touching a header is the number of translation units that reach it, so headers near the bottom of the include graph (core types, geometry, logging) are the expensive ones. A useful audit computes, for every header, its count of dependent translation units and looks at the largest.

In the example, geom.h has 3 dependents, db.h has 2, net.h and timer.h have 1 each: geom.h is the hot spot. Remedies are structural. Forward declarations let a header mention a type without including its definition. Splitting a large header separates rarely changing interfaces from frequently changing details. Keeping implementation out of headers, rather than in inline functions and templates, stops internal edits from rippling outward. These are the same narrow-interface rules that make an engine easy to extend: a plug-in that compiles against a small, stable header rebuilds in seconds when only the plug-in changes.

## Going deeper

Lakos, "Large-Scale C++ Software Design" (1996) and "Large-Scale C++, Volume I" (2019); the Ninja and CMake documentation; Mokhov, Mitchell and Peyton Jones, "Build Systems à la Carte" (ICFP 2018).

A developer edits log.h. How many translation units must an incremental build recompile?
problems.e: A translation unit depends on every header it includes directly or through other headers. The units that reach log.h are cts.cpp and parse_def.cpp: 2 recompiles.

label: Continuous integration for EDA tools
lesson:
# Continuous integration for EDA tools

Continuous integration builds the tool and runs its tests on every proposed change, before it merges. For EDA tools the tests are expensive: a regression design takes minutes to hours, and the meaningful checks are QoR comparisons against baselines, not just pass or fail. A CI pipeline therefore has to be engineered like a parallel job: sharded across runners to meet a time budget, tiered so cheap checks run first, and robust against flaky tests that fail without a real bug.

## Wall time of a sharded test stage

A test stage with $N$ designs of $t$ minutes each, spread over $R$ runners, gives each runner at most $\lceil N/R \rceil$ designs. Each runner usually first builds or downloads the tool, a fixed setup time $S$. The stage wall time is
$$W = S + \left\lceil \frac{N}{R} \right\rceil t.$$
Example: 30 designs of 4 min on 6 runners with 8 min of setup: $8 + 5 \times 4 = 28$ min. On 12 runners: $8 + 3 \times 4 = 20$ min. Setup is paid on every runner in parallel, so it bounds the wall time from below and becomes the main cost as runners are added. Building the tool once and sharing the binary as a CI artifact turns per-runner setup into a download, and real suites balance shards by measured design run times rather than by count.

## Runners needed to meet a budget

Given a budget $B$ minutes, the stage fits if $S + \lceil N/R \rceil t \le B$, that is, if each runner gets at most $K = \lfloor (B - S)/t \rfloor$ designs. The fewest runners is then $R = \lceil N/K \rceil$.

Example: a pull-request check must finish in 30 min, with 45 designs of 5 min and 10 min of setup. $K = \lfloor 20/5 \rfloor = 4$ designs per runner, so $R = \lceil 45/4 \rceil = 12$ runners, which gives $10 + 4 \times 5 = 30$ min. Eleven runners would need 5 designs on some runner, 35 min. When no affordable runner count fits, the suite is tiered: a small, fast set of designs gates every pull request, and the full suite with QoR comparison runs nightly against the main branch.

## Flaky tests and retries

A flaky test fails sometimes on correct code: a timeout on a loaded runner, a race in the test harness, a nondeterministic engine. If $f$ flaky tests each fail independently with probability $q$, a correct commit passes all of them with probability $(1 - q)^f$. With $f = 5$ and $q = 0.05$, that is $0.95^5 \approx 77.38\%$: almost one correct commit in four is blocked.

Rerunning a failed flaky test once, and accepting a pass, cuts its failure probability to $q^2 = 0.0025$, so all five pass with probability $(1 - 0.0025)^5 \approx 98.76\%$. Retries are a stopgap with a cost: they hide nondeterminism that may be a real engine bug, and a test that passes on retry should be logged and fixed. For EDA engines, a QoR test that is flaky usually means the engine is not deterministic, which is exactly the property CI exists to protect.

## Going deeper

Humble and Farley, "Continuous Delivery" (2010); Luo et al., "An Empirical Analysis of Flaky Tests" (FSE 2014); the OpenROAD and OpenROAD-flow-scripts repositories' CI configuration as working examples.

problems.e: Each runner builds for 3 min, then runs at most ceil(19/3) = 7 designs of 5 min: 3 + 35 = 38 min.

label: Version control and bisecting regressions
lesson:
# Version control and bisecting regressions

Version control gives every state of the tool a name, a commit, and lets anyone rebuild any of them. That turns a regression into a search problem: if last week's build was good and today's is bad, the culprit is one of the commits in between. Bisection finds it by binary search over history. For EDA tools, where each test means building the tool and running a design for many minutes, the logarithmic cost of bisection is the difference between an hour and a week.

## Halving the suspect range

Suppose $n$ commits separate a known good build from a known bad one, so the first bad commit is one of $n$ suspects, the bad endpoint included. Bisection tests the middle suspect: if it is bad, the culprit is at or before it; if good, after it. Each test halves the range, so identifying the culprit takes at most
$$\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$$
tests. Example: 200 commits between a good and a bad nightly need $\lceil \log_2 200 \rceil = 8$ tests, since $2^7 = 128 < 200 \le 256 = 2^8$.

Git automates the bookkeeping: git bisect checks out the midpoint, the engineer or a script marks it good or bad, and it proposes the next commit. A script that builds the tool, runs the design and compares a QoR threshold can drive the whole search unattended. The test must be deterministic, or a noisy QoR measure will steer bisection the wrong way.

## Time to find the culprit

Each bisection step costs a build and a test run, so the worst-case time is
$$T = \lceil \log_2 n \rceil\,(t_{build} + t_{test}).$$
Example: 200 suspects, a 15 min build and a 40 min design run: $8 \times 55 = 440$ min, just over 7 hours, unattended. Reducing either term pays off 8 times: a compiler cache that cuts the build to 5 min saves 80 min, and a smaller design that still shows the regression saves far more.

Two practical complications. Some commits do not build, or fail for an unrelated reason; bisection can skip them, at the cost of possibly ending with a small range rather than one commit. And a regression may need two commits to interact, which a single bisection cannot isolate. Keeping commits small and individually buildable is what makes history searchable.

## Bisection against a linear scan

A linear scan tests suspects one by one, oldest first. If the first $n - 1$ all pass, the last one is the culprit without testing it, so the worst case is $n - 1$ tests, against $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ for bisection.

For 200 suspects, that is 199 tests against 8: 191 extra build-and-run cycles, or several days at 55 min each. The gap grows quickly, since doubling the range adds only one bisection step. The comparison also explains why per-commit CI matters even though bisection is efficient: a regression caught on the commit that introduced it needs no search at all, while a regression found weeks later, across thousands of commits by many authors, still costs a dozen expensive steps and a confusing history. Nightly QoR tracking sits in between: it bounds the search to one day's commits, typically a few dozen.

## Going deeper

Chacon and Straub, "Pro Git" (2nd ed.), section on git bisect; Zeller, "Why Programs Fail" (2nd ed., 2009), chapter on delta debugging.

label: C++ and Rust in EDA
lesson:
# C++ and Rust in EDA

Almost every production EDA engine, commercial or open source, has a C++ core: OpenROAD, OpenSTA, Yosys, KLayout, Verilator and Xyce among them. The choice is not fashion. Engines touch hundreds of millions of objects in tight loops and need control of memory layout and native speed. C++ also brings use-after-free bugs, data races and a fragile binary interface. Rust is increasingly used for new components because it removes whole classes of these bugs at compile time, and real tools increasingly mix the two, which makes the boundary between languages a design problem.

## Why EDA cores are written in C++

Three properties keep C++ at the core. Performance: compiled native code, templates that the compiler instantiates and inlines per type, and no interpreter or garbage collector between the algorithm and memory. Layout control: the engineer decides whether instances live in arrays of structures or structures of arrays, uses 32-bit ids instead of 64-bit pointers, and pools allocations, which decides cache behaviour on large designs. Ecosystem: decades of EDA code, libraries and expertise.

The costs are equally concrete. Manual memory management produces dangling pointers, for example a stale pointer to an instance that an optimizer deleted. The C++ ABI, including name mangling, class layout and standard-library internals, differs between compilers and versions, so a plug-in built with one toolchain can crash when it receives a std::string from another. Long compile times come from heavy headers and templates. Large EDA code bases control these risks with handle-based object access, sanitizers in CI and narrow C-style plug-in boundaries.

## What Rust's ownership buys

Rust's ownership rules say that every value has one owner, and that at any moment there is either any number of shared references to it or exactly one mutable reference. The compiler enforces this, so safe Rust code cannot use freed memory and cannot have data races: a router that shares a read-only grid among threads and gives each thread exclusive mutable access to its own region compiles, while one in which two threads could write the same cell does not.

Rust does not make an engine deterministic: floating-point reductions in timing-dependent order still vary, which remains the programmer's job. And single ownership fits cyclic pointer graphs badly; a netlist where nets point to pins and pins point back to nets is awkward with references. Rust EDA code therefore usually stores objects in arenas or vectors and refers to them by integer index, the same id-based pattern good C++ databases use, which also happens to be cache friendly.

## Crossing language boundaries

Real tools mix languages: a C++ core, Tcl and Python for scripting, and increasingly Rust components. Every boundary needs a contract. OpenROAD exposes its C++ engines to Tcl and Python through wrappers generated by SWIG, glue code that converts arguments and wraps native objects in script handles. A script that keeps a handle to an instance the engine has since deleted can crash or read garbage unless the binding checks validity, so ownership across the boundary must be designed, for instance by passing ids that are checked on use.

Between Rust and C++, the robust interface is the C ABI: plain structs, explicit create and destroy functions, and no language-specific types such as std::vector or Vec crossing the line. Memory-safety guarantees stop at that boundary; the unsafe wrapper code must uphold lifetimes and aliasing by hand. A rule of thumb for new components: hot per-object loops in C++ or Rust, orchestration and report post-processing in Python.

## Going deeper

Stroustrup, "A Tour of C++" (3rd ed., 2022); Klabnik and Nichols, "The Rust Programming Language" (the Rust book), chapters on ownership and fearless concurrency; the SWIG documentation and OpenROAD's developer guide on its Tcl and Python bindings.

C) C++ programs need no testing

D) Python cannot express graph algorithms
problems.a: They need predictable native speed, control of memory layout and no interpreter overhead per object
problems.e: Engines touch hundreds of millions of objects in tight loops. Native code with controlled layout is orders of magnitude faster than interpreted per-object work.
