label: The SKY130 open PDK
prereqs: What a process design kit contains
lesson:
# The SKY130 open PDK

SKY130 is the SkyWater 130 nm process, released as an open process design kit with Google's backing. It was the first open PDK that a full digital flow could target end to end, so it is where most open-source EDA tools are tested and compared. For a tool builder it is a real process to read, parse and run against: every view a commercial flow consumes exists here in open form.

## What the SKY130 kit contains

A PDK is the process described in files. SKY130 ships SPICE device models (for ngspice and Xyce), the layer definitions and design rules, DRC and LVS decks for open verifiers such as Magic, KLayout and Netgen, and libraries built on the process: standard cells, IO cells and some primitive devices. Each library cell comes in several views: a GDS layout, a LEF abstract, Liberty timing and power models per corner, a SPICE netlist and a Verilog model. What the PDK does not contain is anything specific to your design: RTL, SDC, floorplan choices and flow parameters are yours. When two people disagree about a DRC or timing result on the same layout, the first thing to compare is the PDK version, because rule decks, models and libraries evolve between releases. A flow that does not pin its PDK version is not reproducible.

## The SKY130 layer stack and libraries

SKY130 has a local-interconnect layer, li1, below five metal layers named met1 to met5. Standard cells use li1 for their internal wiring, which leaves more of met1 free for routing. Higher layers are thicker and less resistive, so they suit long wires and the power grid. Several standard-cell libraries share the process, named like sky130_fd_sc_hd: fd marking a foundry-provided library, sc for standard cell, and a suffix for the variant. hd is high density, hs is high speed, and there are others for low power, low leakage and different voltages. They trade cell height, transistor width and leakage, so the same RTL maps to different area and speed. A worked choice: a small controller with a relaxed 50 MHz clock and a tight area budget goes to hd. A datapath that misses timing at hd may close in hs, at the price of more area and leakage.

## How a flow consumes SKY130

Each flow stage reads the view it needs. Synthesis (Yosys and ABC) reads Liberty to know cell functions, area and delay. Placement and routing read the technology LEF (layers, vias, sites) and the cell LEF (size, pins, obstructions); they never touch transistor geometry. The static timer reads Liberty for the chosen corner, and extraction uses the layer stack to compute parasitics. At the end the flow replaces each LEF abstract with the cell's GDS (ORFS does this with KLayout), and the DRC and LVS decks check the merged layout. Two common mistakes come straight from this division. A final GDS with empty boxes where cells should be means the merge step did not run. Timing that looks too good often means a fast-corner Liberty was loaded, for example an ff file instead of tt, so every arc is faster than the corner you meant to sign off.

## Going deeper

The SkyWater SKY130 PDK documentation; the open_pdks installer documentation; the OpenROAD-flow-scripts platform files for sky130hd.

problems.a: Layout verifiers such as KLayout, Magic and Netgen
problems.e: Rule decks drive physical verification. Placement, synthesis and timing use LEF and Liberty instead.

label: GF180MCU and IHP SG13G2
lesson:
# GF180MCU and IHP SG13G2

SKY130 is not the only open process. GF180MCU from GlobalFoundries and SG13G2 from IHP widen the choice: one aimed at mixed-voltage microcontroller-class designs, the other at SiGe BiCMOS for RF and high-speed analog. A tool builder who supports more than one PDK learns quickly which parts of a flow are process-neutral and which must be replaced, which is exactly the separation a good flow architecture enforces.

## GF180MCU for mixed-voltage designs

GF180MCU is a 180 nm process for microcontroller-class designs, released as an open PDK by GlobalFoundries. Its distinguishing trait is device options for several supply voltages, including higher-voltage devices useful for interfacing with 5 V signals, which the newer, thinner-oxide nodes cannot tolerate. It offers standard-cell libraries at more than one track height. Taller cells hold wider transistors and more internal routing room, so they drive larger loads and route more easily, but each cell costs more area. At 180 nm, digital density is low compared with modern nodes, so it suits control logic, sensor interfaces and mixed-signal glue rather than large datapaths. Moving a flow from SKY130 to GF180MCU breaks anything tied to the old site: row height, site name, tapcell spacing, PDN pitch and routing-layer names all change.

## IHP SG13G2 for SiGe BiCMOS and RF

IHP SG13G2 is a 130 nm SiGe BiCMOS process with an open PDK. BiCMOS means it offers both CMOS transistors and bipolar transistors on one die. The bipolar devices are silicon-germanium heterojunction bipolar transistors (HBTs), which switch far faster than the process's MOSFETs and are the reason the process exists: low-noise amplifiers, mixers, oscillators and high-speed drivers at frequencies well into the tens of gigahertz. Its metal stack includes thick top metals with low sheet resistance, which raise inductor quality factor and lower loss on RF lines and power routes. Because it is BiCMOS, it also has a CMOS standard-cell library, so a digital flow runs on it and RF and control logic can share a chip. The digital density is that of a 130 nm process, so a large digital block costs real area.

## Choosing and porting between open PDKs

Choose a PDK by its hardest requirement. Dense digital logic at modest speed: SKY130. Higher-voltage interfaces: GF180MCU. RF or very high-speed analog: SG13G2, accepting lower digital density. Then port the flow. Every physical and timing view comes from the PDK: technology LEF, cell LEF, Liberty per corner, cell GDS, SPICE models, and the DRC and LVS decks. On top of these, a flow keeps per-platform settings such as layer directions, PDN straps, tapcell rules, fill rules and the default routing layers. Well-structured flows keep these in a platform directory, separate from each design's configuration, which only names the platform. Then rerunning a design on another process is a one-line change in the design config, plus whatever the design itself must adapt to (a new clock target, a different IO ring).

## Going deeper

The GF180MCU and IHP SG13G2 open PDK repositories and their documentation; the OpenROAD-flow-scripts platform directories.

problems.a: More area for stronger drive and easier routing
problems.e: Taller cells hold wider transistors and more internal routing room, so they drive harder and route more easily but cost area.

label: What open access does not give you
lesson:
# What open access does not give you

Open PDKs and open tools let anyone design a chip and verify it. They do not, on their own, turn that design into a product. Knowing exactly where the open release stops matters for anyone who builds tools on it, because a tool that reports clean DRC or positive slack on an open PDK is reporting evidence under assumptions, not a guarantee of working, manufacturable, qualified silicon.

## What the open PDK files do not include

An open PDK releases rules, device models, layer data and basic libraries. It usually does not release the foundry's production yield data, statistical correlation between models and silicon lots, or a portfolio of complex, silicon-qualified IP: high-speed SerDes, PLLs, qualified SRAM compilers, and certified IO and ESD libraries. Some of these exist as open projects, for example open SRAM generators, but their models may not be validated across corners. Open DRC and LVS decks may also lag or simplify the foundry's internal signoff decks, so a layout clean under the open deck may still violate a rule the foundry checks. Treat open results as strong evidence within the encoded rules and models. When a design depends on something the release lacks, the risk is the designer's, and a tool should say which inputs were assumed.

## From open files to fabricated silicon

A verified GDS is not a chip. Mask making and wafer processing happen at a mask shop and the foundry, and they need a fabrication run. Open designs usually reach silicon through multi-project shuttles: many small designs share one mask set and one wafer run, which divides the dominant fixed cost, the masks, among all participants. Each project gets a handful of packaged or bare dies back. Prototypes that work at room temperature prove the design concept. A product still needs reliability qualification across temperature and voltage, a production test program, packaging qualification, and a supply agreement for volume. None of these comes from open files. A tool builder working on open flows should be clear that the flow ends at a verified handoff; the rest of the path is a business and engineering process with the foundry.

## Engineering around the gaps

Good practice on an open PDK is conservative. Reuse the IO cells the PDK provides rather than drawing new pad circuits, since ESD design depends on silicon data you do not have. Add timing margin beyond the reported slack: if the libraries have not been correlated to measured silicon, model error is unknown, and a guard band of a few percent of the clock period is cheap insurance. Choose modest clock targets and layouts that stay well inside the characterized range. Cross-check physical verification with two independent engines, such as Magic and KLayout. For research that should inform a commercial product, carry over methods and relative comparisons (algorithm A beats algorithm B by 4% wirelength on the same process) rather than absolute numbers, which do not transfer between processes and decks.

## Going deeper

The documentation of open shuttle programs and of the SKY130, GF180MCU and SG13G2 PDKs; Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design" (4th ed.), chapters on manufacturing and test.

problems.a: It may not be silicon-validated across corners
problems.e: Open memory compilers are valuable but often lack the silicon characterization a commercial memory brings. Treat their models with caution.

label: Yosys and ABC in an open flow
lesson:
# Yosys and ABC in an open flow

Every open digital flow starts with Yosys, which reads Verilog, elaborates and optimizes it in its RTLIL intermediate representation, and hands the combinational logic to ABC for optimization and technology mapping against a Liberty library. A tool builder needs the script's structure, the exact handoff between the two tools, and the common failure signatures, because synthesis problems surface downstream as strange placement or timing.

## The shape of a Yosys synthesis script

A typical open-flow script reads the Verilog, then runs hierarchy with the top module named, which elaborates parameters and reports undefined modules. proc lowers always blocks into explicit multiplexers, flip-flops and latches. opt, fsm and memory passes simplify logic, extract and recode state machines, and map memories. techmap lowers generic cells into a fine-grained gate library. dfflibmap with the Liberty file maps the internal flip-flop cells onto real library flip-flops. abc with the Liberty file maps the remaining combinational logic. opt_clean removes dangling wires and cells, and write_verilog emits the structural netlist. Flows add passes for their downstream tools, such as tie-cell insertion for constants or buffer insertion for direct port-to-port assigns. Yosys also has a synth command that bundles a standard sequence; open flows usually write the steps out to control them.

## What ABC receives and returns

When Yosys runs abc, it extracts the combinational logic, writes it out for ABC, and reads the mapped result back, stitching it into the netlist between the flip-flops and other cells Yosys keeps. ABC represents logic internally as and-inverter graphs, optimizes them with rewriting, refactoring and balancing, then maps to the library using each cell's Boolean function, area and delay from the Liberty file. Geometry from LEF and clocks from SDC never enter. If a flow passes a clock period or delay target, ABC favors faster structures, often at more area; without one, it leans toward area. An example: a 32-bit adder mapped with no target tends toward a compact, slower structure; with an aggressive target ABC spends more cells to shorten the critical path, and the reported area rises.

## Diagnosing open synthesis failures

Three failures recur. First, "module not defined" for an SRAM or other hard macro: there is no RTL to synthesize, so the flow must supply a blackbox declaration or a Liberty model so Yosys keeps the instance as a black box. Second, a netlist far smaller than expected, with outputs tied to constants: logic that drives no observable output is legally removed, so an unconnected port, a typo in a port name or a missing keep attribute shows up as missing logic. Third, large area differences between two Liberty files from one PDK: mapping can only use the cells offered, so a library with richer complex gates or different sizes changes the result. A fourth, softer symptom is a netlist with plain assigns between ports that a physical tool rejects; flows insert buffers to give every connection a driving cell.

## Going deeper

The Yosys manual (passes proc, techmap, dfflibmap, abc); the ABC documentation and Mishchenko's papers on AIG rewriting and mapping; the OpenROAD-flow-scripts synthesis scripts.

problems.e: dfflibmap maps internal flip-flop cells to Liberty flip-flops. abc handles the combinational logic.

label: The OpenROAD tool suite
prereqs: The RTL-to-GDSII flow end to end
lesson:
# The OpenROAD tool suite

OpenROAD is one application that links a set of physical-design tools onto one OpenDB database, driven from a Tcl shell or Python. Each tool has a short name and one job: initialize the floorplan, place pins, build the power grid, place cells, repair timing, build the clock tree, route, extract and time. Knowing which tool owns which job, and what it leaves in the database for the next, is the map a tool builder needs before modifying any of them.

## Floorplan and placement tools

ifp initializes the floorplan: it sets die and core areas, either explicitly or from a target utilization, and builds rows of sites from the library's site definition. ppl places top-level IO pins on the die boundary, usually to shorten wires to the cells they connect to. tapcell inserts well taps and endcaps that the process requires, and pdn builds the power distribution network of rings, straps and rails. gpl is the global placer, from the RePlAce line of electrostatics-based placers: it treats cells as charges, solves for a density potential, and moves cells with a Nesterov-type method toward low wirelength and uniform density. Its result still overlaps. dpl, the detailed placer, snaps every cell to a legal site in a row without overlap and makes local improvements. Each tool reads and writes the same database, so the next tool simply sees the updated objects.

## Optimization, clock and routing tools

rsz, the resizer, runs repair design (fixing maximum slew, capacitance and fanout by buffering and sizing) and repair timing (sizing and buffering to fix setup and hold). cts, from TritonCTS, builds a buffered clock tree toward balanced latency at the flip-flop clock pins. grt, the global router from the FastRoute line, divides the die into gcells, assigns each net a path through them and through layers, and reports congestion as demand versus capacity per gcell edge. It writes route guides. drt, from TritonRoute, turns guides into exact wires and vias that obey the design rules, iterating with rip-up and reroute and reporting any violations it cannot fix. Order matters: grt's guides confine drt's search, and the clock tree must exist before signal routing claims the tracks near the flip-flops.

## Extraction, timing and the shared database

OpenRCX extracts resistance and capacitance from the routed geometry using calibrated rules and writes them as SPEF or loads them for timing. OpenSTA is the static timer: it reads Liberty and SDC and times the design using estimated or extracted parasitics. Because all tools live in one process on one database, a tool can call another without writing a file. The resizer asks OpenSTA for slack after every batch of edits; a timing-driven gpl run asks for net criticality between iterations and reweights nets; global routing can feed estimated parasitics back to the timer. In a flow of separate point tools, each of those exchanges would be a DEF and SPEF write and read, minutes on a large design. This is why OpenROAD's architecture is a shared in-memory database with tools as modules, and why an incremental timer is part of it.

## Going deeper

The OpenROAD documentation for each tool (ifp, ppl, pdn, gpl, rsz, dpl, cts, grt, drt, OpenRCX, OpenSTA); Ajayi et al. on the OpenROAD project.

problems.q:

B) grt, the global router

C) ppl, the pin placer

D) gpl, the global placer
problems.a: dpl, the detailed placer
problems.e: dpl legalizes and refines placement so each cell sits on a site in a row with no overlaps.

problems.q:

C) dpl, the detailed placer

D) gpl, the global placer
problems.a: ifp, the floorplan initializer
problems.e: ifp initializes the floorplan from a utilization or explicit die area and builds rows from the library site.

problems.q:

A) grt, the global router

B) dpl, the detailed placer

C) gpl, the global placer

D) ppl, the pin placer
problems.a: dpl, the detailed placer
problems.e: dpl legalizes and refines placement so each cell sits on a site in a row with no overlaps.

problems.q:

A) drt, the detailed router

B) OpenSTA, the timer

C) grt, the global router

D) gpl, the global placer
problems.a: grt, the global router
problems.e: grt is global routing from the FastRoute line. It produces route guides and congestion data.

problems.q:

A) cts, from TritonCTS

B) drt, from TritonRoute

C) pdn, the power-grid generator

D) grt, from FastRoute
problems.a: cts, from TritonCTS
problems.e: cts builds a buffered clock tree toward balanced latency at the sinks.

problems.q:

A) gpl, the global placer

B) drt, the detailed router

C) grt, the global router

D) OpenSTA, the timer
problems.a: grt, the global router
problems.e: grt is global routing from the FastRoute line. It produces route guides and congestion data.

problems.q:

A) From drt to grt

B) From cts to ppl

C) From gpl to ifp

D) From grt to drt
problems.a: From grt to drt
problems.e: Global routing produces guides that confine the detailed router's search.

problems.q:

problems.a: OpenSTA runs inside the same process on the same database
problems.e: OpenROAD links its tools into one application over one OpenDB, so the timer sees edits immediately.

problems.e: Because tools share the database and process, the placer can ask the timer for criticality and reweight nets as it goes.

label: OpenROAD-flow-scripts

lesson:
# OpenROAD-flow-scripts

OpenROAD-flow-scripts (ORFS) is the reference flow around OpenROAD: Makefiles and scripts that take a design from Verilog to GDS on several platforms. It runs six stages, synth, floorplan, place, cts, route and finish, each a set of steps whose order is forced by what each step needs from the ones before. A tool builder uses ORFS to reproduce results, to locate where a QoR change came from, and as a harness for new engines.

## Stages and what belongs to each

The synth stage runs Yosys and ABC to produce a gate-level netlist. The floorplan stage initializes the die and core from a utilization or explicit area, places macros, inserts tapcells and endcaps, and generates the power distribution network. The place stage runs global placement, places the IO pins, places again with the pins fixed, repairs the design by resizing and buffering, and runs detailed placement. The cts stage builds the clock tree and then repairs timing now that clock latencies are real, legalizing the cells it moved. The route stage runs global routing and then detailed routing, and inserts filler cells. The finish stage performs metal fill if the platform asks for it, writes the final reports, and merges the cell layouts into the final GDS with KLayout. Each stage saves its database under results, so a run can resume or be inspected stage by stage.

## Ordering the steps

To order a set of steps, first place each in its stage, then order steps inside a stage by data dependence. Example: the steps detailed routing, clock tree synthesis, PDN generation, repair design and global placement. By stage: PDN generation is floorplan; global placement and repair design are place; clock tree synthesis is cts; detailed routing is route. Inside place, repair design follows global placement because buffering needs cell locations to estimate wire loads. So the order is PDN generation, global placement, repair design, clock tree synthesis, detailed routing. A typical wrong option swaps two adjacent steps, for example clock tree synthesis before repair design, which looks plausible but would build a tree on a netlist that is about to change.

## Why the order is forced

The order is not convention; each step consumes an artifact of the previous one. Placement needs the rows and the power grid from the floorplan, because rails define where cells can sit. Repair design needs placed cells to estimate wire capacitance. Clock tree synthesis needs final flip-flop locations, otherwise the tree's balance is computed for the wrong sinks. Timing repair after CTS needs real clock latencies, which only exist once the tree is built. Global routing needs the clock tree's buffers and wires in place, and detailed routing needs global routing's guides. The finish stage needs every wire to compute fill and to write a complete GDS. So the step immediately after clock tree synthesis among a drawn set is the next one whose input it produces, here post-CTS timing repair if it was drawn, otherwise the earliest routing step in the set.

## Going deeper

The OpenROAD-flow-scripts documentation and its Makefile and stage scripts; the OpenROAD tool documentation.

problems.e: "repair design (resizing and buffering)" is in the place stage, the earliest stage among these steps, and cells must have locations before a clock tree can be built to their clock pins.

label: The GCD design as a first run
prereqs: Rows, sites and the placement region
lesson:
# The GCD design as a first run

GCD, a small greatest-common-divisor circuit, is the design every new ORFS user runs first. It is small enough to finish in minutes yet exercises every stage, so it validates the installation and gives a baseline. A first run teaches the configuration file, the floorplan arithmetic that turns utilization into a core, and where the results land, which is the foundation for every later experiment on larger designs.

## The design configuration

Each design in ORFS has a config.mk per platform, under designs/<platform>/<design>/. For GCD it sets DESIGN_NAME (the top module), PLATFORM, VERILOG_FILES (the RTL), and SDC_FILE (the constraints, which define the clock). Two knobs shape the physical result. CORE_UTILIZATION sets how much of the core area the standard cells should fill, as a percentage; the floorplan derives the core from it. PLACE_DENSITY sets the target density that global placement spreads cells toward. Everything about the process, such as layers, rows, PDN and libraries, comes from the platform's own files, which is why the same GCD runs on several platforms by changing one path. Running the flow is a make invocation that names the design's config; it then executes the six stages in order.

## Sizing the core from utilization

Utilization is cell area divided by core area, so the core area is $A_{core} = A_{cells}/u$. Example: GCD on sky130hd synthesizes to 2400 square microns of cells and CORE_UTILIZATION is 45, so $A_{core} = 2400/0.45 = 5333.3$ square microns. A square core has side $\sqrt{5333.3} = 73.03$ microns. The sky130hd row height is 2.72 microns, so $\lfloor 73.03/2.72 \rfloor = 26$ whole rows fit. Rows on nangate45 are 1.4 microns tall and on asap7 0.27 microns, so the same arithmetic gives very different row counts. Common slips are multiplying by the utilization instead of dividing, which shrinks the core below the cells' own area, and forgetting the square root. The real floorplan also snaps the core to the site grid and leaves a margin between core and die for the power ring and IO.

## Reading the first results

ORFS writes everything per platform and design: logs/ holds each step's log, reports/ holds timing, area and power reports, results/ holds stage databases, netlists and the final GDS, and objects/ holds intermediate files such as the prepared libraries. Read the final report first: worst and total negative slack, design area and utilization, power, and DRC count after routing. If setup slack is negative, the target being missed is the clock period in the SDC; relax it or let the repair steps work harder. If global routing reports overflow, demand exceeds track supply, so lower CORE_UTILIZATION to give the router space. Finally, run it twice: identical inputs should give identical results, and that reproducible baseline is what every later change is judged against.

## Going deeper

The OpenROAD-flow-scripts tutorial and documentation for the GCD design and config.mk variables.

label: OpenLane 2
lesson:
# OpenLane 2

OpenLane 2 is a Python infrastructure for building RTL-to-GDS flows out of steps, the successor of the original OpenLane. It does not contain its own placer or router; it orchestrates Yosys, OpenROAD, KLayout, Magic, Netgen and other tools on open PDKs. For a tool builder it is a second, differently shaped harness next to ORFS, and a model for how to make a flow extensible.

## Flows built from steps

In OpenLane 2 a step wraps one action, such as running synthesis, global placement or a DRC check. Each step declares the design views it consumes and produces: netlists, ODB databases, DEF, SPEF, GDS and reports. A flow is a sequence of steps, and the state of views passes from one to the next, so a later step starts where the earlier ones left off. Flows are written in Python, which makes it natural to add a custom step, for example a checker that inspects placement density before clock tree synthesis, or to build a new flow that reuses existing steps in a different order. The configuration supplies the design's files and parameters, and per-PDK defaults fill in the rest. This structure is the flow-level version of a plug-in architecture: well-defined interfaces between steps make the pieces replaceable.

## How OpenLane 2 relates to OpenROAD, Yosys and PDKs

OpenLane 2 calls the same engines ORFS calls. Synthesis steps run Yosys with ABC. Floorplanning, placement, clock tree synthesis, resizing, routing, extraction and timing run OpenROAD's tools on OpenDB. Physical verification runs Magic or KLayout with the PDK's DRC decks, and Netgen compares the extracted layout netlist with the gate netlist for LVS. The PDK, for example SKY130 or GF180MCU, supplies the views and the per-PDK settings; OpenLane holds no process technology of its own. A consequence for debugging: when a routing step produces bad wires, the code responsible is OpenROAD's router, and OpenLane's role is how it invoked it, which parameters and inputs it passed. Reproducing the step's tool invocation outside the flow is the fastest way to tell an orchestration bug from an engine bug.

## Choosing between OpenLane 2 and ORFS

Both are orchestration layers over the same engines, so the choice is about workflow. ORFS is developed alongside OpenROAD, is driven by Makefiles and Tcl stage scripts, and exposes OpenROAD's commands directly, which suits engine development and reproducing OpenROAD results. OpenLane 2 offers a Python API for composing flows from steps, plus configuration conventions and checks, which suits building custom flows and integrating new checks. On the same design and PDK, the two may report different QoR: default utilization, density, repair settings, routing layers and signoff checks differ, so the recipes differ even though the engines do not. A fair comparison fixes those knobs to the same values, or reports each flow's settings beside its numbers.

## Going deeper

The OpenLane 2 documentation (steps, flows and configuration); the OpenROAD-flow-scripts documentation.

label: KLayout, Magic and Netgen
lesson:
# KLayout, Magic and Netgen

After routing, the open flow turns to layout tools: KLayout to view, check and merge GDS, Magic to edit layout, check rules and extract circuits, and Netgen to compare netlists for LVS. These are the open counterparts of commercial physical verification, and a tool builder needs to know what each consumes, what it proves, and how to read a disagreement between them.

## KLayout for viewing, DRC and GDS merging

KLayout is a fast hierarchical layout viewer and editor for GDS and OASIS. GDS stores layers as numbers, so a layer-properties file maps each layer and datatype pair to a name and color; without it a SKY130 layout shows as anonymous numbers. KLayout's DRC engine runs rule decks written as scripts that express layer derivations and checks, such as width, spacing and enclosure, and it also supports LVS decks. In ORFS the finish stage uses KLayout to merge: the routed design references cells only as LEF abstracts, and KLayout replaces each reference with the cell's real GDS layout to write the final stream. Its hierarchical handling is why it opens very large layouts quickly: a cell drawn once and placed ten thousand times is stored once.

## Magic for layout, DRC and extraction

Magic is a VLSI layout editor with built-in, incremental DRC and circuit extraction, and it is widely used for SKY130 work. Its extraction turns layout into a SPICE netlist of devices and, optionally, parasitic resistance and capacitance, which feeds both LVS and post-layout circuit simulation. Many open flows run DRC in both Magic and KLayout, because the decks are written independently and one may encode a rule that the other misses or interprets differently. When they disagree, for example Magic flags a met2 spacing that KLayout passes, do not take the clean result as the answer: inspect the geometry at the marker, read the rule in both decks, and decide which encoding matches the process rule.

## Netgen for LVS

Netgen performs LVS by comparing two netlists: the one extracted from layout (by Magic or KLayout) and the source netlist from the design. It matches devices and connectivity as a graph comparison, iteratively partitioning devices and nets until each class matches one to one or a mismatch is isolated. Reading its report is a skill. Two source nets that appear as one layout net mean a short. One source net split into two layout nets means an open. A mismatch confined to power pins often means naming differences or implicit power connections in one netlist. Device-property mismatches, such as transistor width, point to layout that differs from what was intended. Because Netgen compares netlists, a broken extraction setup makes every comparison fail; checking extraction on a single known-good cell first saves time.

## Going deeper

The KLayout documentation on DRC and LVS scripting; the Magic and Netgen documentation by R. Timothy Edwards; the SKY130 PDK verification setup.

label: Open simulators and formal tools
lesson:
# Open simulators and formal tools

Open EDA has a full verification toolbox: Verilator and cocotb for fast digital simulation with Python testbenches, SymbiYosys for formal proofs, and ngspice, Xyce and Xschem for transistor-level work. Knowing which tool answers which question, and what each one's model leaves out, keeps a tool builder from trusting a result that the tool was never able to produce.

## Digital simulation with Verilator and cocotb

Verilator compiles synthesizable Verilog and SystemVerilog into an optimized C++ model that is evaluated cycle by cycle, which makes it one of the fastest open simulators for large designs. Its default model is two-state: unknown values become 0 or 1, optionally randomized, so a test that relies on seeing X propagate from an uninitialized register will not see it. Event-driven simulators such as Icarus Verilog keep four-state values at lower speed. cocotb is a framework for writing testbenches in Python as coroutines that await clock edges and signal changes, driving a simulator underneath. Pairing cocotb with Verilator gives Python's libraries for stimulus and checking with a compiled model's speed. For a regression of thousands of random tests, that combination keeps run time manageable.

## Formal checks with SymbiYosys

SymbiYosys (sby) is a front end that reads a design and its assertions through Yosys and runs SAT- or SMT-based engines on it. In BMC mode it unrolls the design for a fixed depth and searches for a counterexample; a clean BMC run of depth 20 proves only that no violation exists within 20 cycles of reset. Prove mode attempts an unbounded proof, for example by k-induction; success means the property holds in every reachable state. Cover mode searches for a trace that reaches each cover statement, which proves a behavior is possible and catches over-constrained assumptions that make a proof vacuous. A failed proof produces a trace that can be viewed in a waveform viewer and replayed in simulation.

## Circuit simulation with ngspice, Xyce and Xschem

Questions about analog behavior, such as whether a comparator settles within 2 ns or how much a ring oscillator's frequency shifts at the slow corner, need circuit simulation with the PDK's device models. ngspice is the widely used open SPICE-class simulator, and the open PDKs ship models for it. Xyce, from Sandia National Laboratories, is a SPICE-compatible simulator designed for parallel execution on large circuits, which helps with big post-layout netlists. Xschem is schematic capture: draw the circuit with PDK symbols, then export a SPICE netlist for ngspice or Xyce, and later compare it against the layout netlist with Netgen. None of the digital tools above can answer these questions, because their models have no voltages, currents or device physics.

## Going deeper

The Verilator, cocotb and SymbiYosys manuals; the ngspice and Xyce user guides; the Xschem documentation.

label: The four layers in code
lesson:
# The four layers in code

The four-layer engine model (immutable core, strategy or policy, parameters, observation hooks) is only useful if it is visible in the source tree. This concept turns it into code: which classes and files of an OpenROAD-like engine belong to each layer, how the seams between them are built, and where an incoming change request lands. An agent editing an engine needs that map to make the smallest safe change.

## Mapping code to the four layers

In a placer, the core is the code that every result must pass through: the legalizer that guarantees cells sit on legal sites without overlap, the row and site model, and the density and wirelength kernels. Policies are the classes that decide how: a cost function, a move set, an ordering for rip-up in a router, each implementing a common interface and selected by name. Parameters are values read at run time from configuration, such as target density, net weights and iteration limits; changing them needs no recompile. Observation hooks are callbacks or query points where an agent reads live state (overflow per iteration, WNS after an incremental update) and can inject a decision, such as stopping early. A quick test for a piece of code: if a wrong change breaks an invariant, it is core; if it only changes quality, it is policy or parameter.

## Narrow interfaces at the seams

A seam is built as an abstract interface plus a factory that creates implementations by name, so the core depends only on the interface and never on any particular plug-in. Keep the interface narrow: a cost plug-in should receive arrays of the values it needs, such as cell widths, positions and net pins, not a pointer to the whole database, which would let it depend on and mutate anything. Plain data at the boundary is easy to version, test and run in parallel. Keep the hot numerical kernel inside the core and call plug-ins coarsely, once per batch of cells rather than once per cell, so the compiler can still inline and vectorize the inner loop. A seam that passes the world, or that is called a million times per pass, has the shape of an interface but not its benefits.

## Placing a change request

Given a request, ask what must change. "Raise the congestion weight from 0.3 to 0.5 on this design" changes a value: a parameter, no recompile. "Keep macros 20 microns from the die edge" adds behavior; if the constraint system has an extension point, it is a policy plug-in written against that interface, and the core is untouched. "Stop global placement when overflow falls below 10%" needs live state and a control: an observation hook. "Change what counts as a legal site" alters the core invariant, so it is a core edit that needs human approval and full regression. If requests of some common kind keep landing in the core, the seam is in the wrong place, and the fix is to move that variability behind a new extension point once, under review.

## Going deeper

The agent-first engine notes in this curriculum (agent_first_eda); the OpenROAD source tree as an example of tools as modules over one database; Ousterhout, "A Philosophy of Software Design", on deep modules.

In an OpenROAD-like placer, which code belongs in the immutable core?

A) The legalizer that guarantees overlap-free cells on legal sites

B) A cost function for abutting regular cells

C) A Tcl hook that prints density each iteration

D) The weight on timing-driven net criticality
problems.a: The legalizer that guarantees overlap-free cells on legal sites
problems.e: Legality is an invariant every result must satisfy, so it lives in the core. Weights are parameters, hooks observe, cost functions are policies.

problems.q:
The placer's target density is read from a config file at run time. Which layer is it?

A) Strategy or policy

B) Parameters

C) Immutable core

D) Observation hooks
problems.a: Parameters
problems.e: A value that changes behavior without recompiling is a parameter.

problems.q:
A router's rip-up-and-reroute ordering is implemented as a class selected by name at startup. Which layer is it?

A) Immutable core

B) Strategy or policy

C) Observation hooks

D) Parameters
problems.a: Strategy or policy
problems.e: A selectable heuristic that decides how the engine searches is policy.

A) The core depends only on a small stable interface, not on each plug-in

B) Abstract classes remove the need for tests

C) Factories make code run faster than direct calls

D) It lets plug-ins change the core's invariants
problems.a: The core depends only on a small stable interface, not on each plug-in
problems.e: A narrow interface and a factory decouple the core from implementations, so new plug-ins never force core edits.

problems.q:
Why should the hot numerical kernel stay inside the core rather than behind a plug-in call?

A) So the compiler can inline and vectorize it

B) Because kernels cannot be tested

C) So plug-ins can replace it per cell

D) Because cores cannot call functions
problems.a: So the compiler can inline and vectorize it
problems.e: Crossing a seam per element blocks inlining and vectorization. Keep the kernel in the core and call plug-ins coarsely.

problems.q:
Why should the hot numerical kernel stay inside the core rather than behind a plug-in call?

A) Because cores cannot call functions

B) So plug-ins can replace it per cell

C) So the compiler can inline and vectorize it

D) Because kernels cannot be tested
problems.a: So the compiler can inline and vectorize it
problems.e: Crossing a seam per element blocks inlining and vectorization. Keep the kernel in the core and call plug-ins coarsely.

problems.q:
A customer asks to raise the congestion weight from 0.3 to 0.5 for one design. Where does the change land?

A) A parameter change, with no recompile

B) A new policy plug-in

C) A core edit with human approval

D) A new observation hook
problems.a: A parameter change, with no recompile
problems.e: Changing an existing weight is configuration, the smallest tier.

problems.q:
A request requires changing how the legalizer defines a legal site. Where does it land?

A) A parameter change

B) A policy plug-in

C) An observation hook

D) A core edit, needing human approval and full regression
problems.a: A core edit, needing human approval and full regression
problems.e: Legality is the core invariant. Changing it is the rare, approved tier.

problems.q:
A customer wants macros kept 20 microns from the die edge, but the placer has no such rule. The constraint system has an extension point. Where does it land?

A) An observation hook

B) A parameter change

C) A policy plug-in at the constraint extension point

D) A core edit to legalization
problems.a: A policy plug-in at the constraint extension point
problems.e: New behavior at a defined extension point is a plug-in. The core stays untouched.

label: Designing an extension-point ABI
lesson:
# Designing an extension-point ABI

An extension point is only stable if its binary interface is. Plug-ins compiled last month must still load after a core release, plug-ins must not slow the hot loop, and plug-in code must not carry hidden state that breaks determinism or threading. This concept covers the design rules for such an ABI and the arithmetic of the call boundary, which decides whether a plug-in is called per cell or per batch.

## What a frozen extension ABI promises

A frozen ABI promises that a binary built against version 1 keeps loading and working with every later core release of the same major version. That rules out reordering struct fields, changing argument types and removing members. Many systems expose a C ABI even when core and plug-ins are written in C++, because C calling conventions and struct layouts are stable across compilers, while C++ name mangling, vtable layouts and standard-library types vary between compilers and versions. Two habits make evolution possible: begin each extension struct with its size and a version number, so the core knows which fields a plug-in understands, and only append new optional functions or fields at the end. Exceptions should not cross the boundary, since unwinding across modules built by different toolchains is not portable; return error codes.

## Paying for the call boundary

Every call across a seam costs overhead: an indirect call, argument marshalling and, above all, the loss of inlining and vectorization. Suppose a pass evaluates $N = 700{,}000$ cells, the cost work is $w = 26$ ns per cell and each call costs $c = 10$ ns. Calling once per cell pays $N c = 7$ ms of overhead on top of $N w = 18.2$ ms of work. Calling once per batch of $B = 1024$ cells makes $\lceil N/B \rceil = 684$ calls, 6.84 microseconds of overhead. The pass speedup is $\frac{N(w+c)}{Nw + \lceil N/B\rceil c} = \frac{25.2}{18.2068} \approx 1.38$. The real gain is usually larger, because inside a batch the plug-in's own loop can be vectorized, which the per-cell design forbids. The rule follows: coarse calls, per batch, not per cell.

## Plain data and no hidden state

A plug-in should be a pure function of its explicit arguments: read-only input arrays of plain structs, an output array it fills, and no global or static state. Passing a std::vector of internal objects by reference couples the plug-in to layouts that are not ABI-stable; a pointer plus a length to plain structs is. A plug-in that caches the last design in a static variable makes results depend on call history, which breaks determinism, makes golden tests flaky, and races when the core calls it from several threads. A simple diagnostic: call the plug-in on the same batches in a different order, or on several threads. Pure plug-ins give identical results; any difference reveals hidden state. Purity is also what lets the core run a plug-in in a sandboxed process and compare its output to a golden result.

## Going deeper

The agent-first engine notes in this curriculum on seams and extension points; documentation of stable plug-in ABIs such as the C interfaces used by many EDA and compiler projects.

problems.q:
A plug-in compiled against version 1 of an extension ABI stops loading after a minor core release. What promise was broken?

A) The promise that tests always pass

B) The promise that plug-ins are written in Tcl

C) The frozen ABI: layouts and signatures at the seam must not change

D) The promise that the core never gets faster
problems.a: The frozen ABI: layouts and signatures at the seam must not change
problems.e: A frozen ABI means binaries built against it keep working. Changing struct layouts or signatures breaks them.

problems.q:
Why should C++ exceptions not cross a plug-in ABI boundary?

A) Exceptions are always faster than error codes

B) Exceptions make the ABI frozen

C) Exception handling is not portable across compilers and runtimes

D) C++ forbids exceptions in libraries
problems.a: Exception handling is not portable across compilers and runtimes
problems.e: Unwinding across modules built by different toolchains can crash. Return error codes at the seam.

problems.q:
Which change to a published extension interface is safe without a new major version?

A) Adding a new optional function at the end of the table

B) Reordering the existing functions

C) Removing a deprecated field

D) Changing an int argument to a double
problems.a: Adding a new optional function at the end of the table
problems.e: Appending keeps existing offsets and signatures. Reordering, retyping or removing breaks compiled plug-ins.

problems.q:
A placer calls a plug-in cost function at an extension point. Each call across the seam costs 7 ns of overhead (indirect call, argument marshalling, no inlining), and the cost work itself is 11 ns per cell. One pass evaluates 500000 cells. Moving from one call per cell to batches of 512 per call, what is the speedup of the whole pass (overhead plus work)? (Round to 2 decimal places.)

A) 1.64

B) 51.2

C) 1.14

D) 1.63
problems.e: Per-cell: 500000 × (11 + 7) ns. Batched: 500000 × 11 ns of work plus 977 × 7 ns of calls. The ratio is 1.63.

problems.q:
A placer calls a plug-in cost function at an extension point. Each call across the seam costs 7 ns of overhead (indirect call, argument marshalling, no inlining), and the cost work itself is 7 ns per cell. One pass evaluates 900000 cells. Moving from one call per cell to batches of 4096 per call, what is the speedup of the whole pass (overhead plus work)? (Round to 2 decimal places.)

A) 1.5

B) 1.74

C) 2.26

D) 2

E) 409.6
problems.e: Per-cell: 900000 × (7 + 7) ns. Batched: 900000 × 7 ns of work plus 220 × 7 ns of calls. The ratio is 2.

problems.q:
A placer calls a plug-in cost function at an extension point. Each call across the seam costs 10 ns of overhead (indirect call, argument marshalling, no inlining), and the cost work itself is 33 ns per cell. One pass evaluates 400000 cells. If instead the core passes cells in batches of 4096 per call, how much call overhead does one pass pay, in microseconds? (Round to 2 decimal places.)

A) 0.98 microseconds

B) 3.22 microseconds

C) 40.14 microseconds

D) 4000 microseconds
problems.a: 0.98 microseconds
problems.e: ceil(400000 / 4096) = 98 calls × 10 ns = 0.98 microseconds.

problems.q:
A seam passes a plug-in a std::vector of internal Cell objects by reference. Why is that risky for a frozen ABI?

A) The vector and Cell layouts may change between compilers or core versions

B) It makes the plug-in stateless

C) Vectors cannot be passed by reference

D) Plain arrays are always slower
problems.a: The vector and Cell layouts may change between compilers or core versions
problems.e: Standard-library and class layouts are not ABI-stable. Pointers plus lengths to plain structs are.

problems.q:
A seam passes a plug-in a std::vector of internal Cell objects by reference. Why is that risky for a frozen ABI?

A) Plain arrays are always slower

B) The vector and Cell layouts may change between compilers or core versions

C) It makes the plug-in stateless

D) Vectors cannot be passed by reference
problems.a: The vector and Cell layouts may change between compilers or core versions
problems.e: Standard-library and class layouts are not ABI-stable. Pointers plus lengths to plain structs are.

problems.q:
Which design makes a derate plug-in easiest to run on many threads at once?

A) One that reads a global corner variable

B) One that logs to a shared buffer without locks

C) A function of its explicit context arguments with no globals

D) One that caches per-thread results in a static map
problems.a: A function of its explicit context arguments with no globals
problems.e: Reentrant code with explicit inputs is thread-safe by construction.

label: Golden and differential test harnesses
lesson:
# Golden and differential test harnesses

An agent that edits engines needs an automatic judge. A golden harness reruns a fixed suite of designs and compares the candidate build's metrics with stored baselines; a differential check proves that a change moved only what it was meant to move. This concept covers the arithmetic of those comparisons: relative change, tolerance gates and counting unintended movement, the numbers on which a promotion decision rests.

## Relative change against a golden baseline

For a metric such as total wirelength or cell area, the harness reports the relative change $\Delta = (x_{cand} - x_{base})/x_{base} \times 100\%$. Example: baseline area 29,900 square microns, candidate 29,617: $\Delta = -283/29900 \times 100 = -0.95\%$. The sign matters: for area and wirelength smaller is better, for slack larger is better, so a harness stores the preferred direction with each metric. Relative change makes designs of different sizes comparable, which is why it is the input to geometric-mean QoR summaries. For metrics near zero, such as WNS close to 0 ps, relative change explodes, so the harness uses absolute differences in ps instead. Golden values are stored with the engine version and seed that produced them, and are regenerated only on a reviewed baseline update.

## Counting tolerance violations

A QoR gate flags a design when its metric moves outside a tolerance band, in either direction, because an unexplained improvement is as suspicious as a regression. With a 1% band on wirelength and designs aes 76,900 → 78,669 (+2.30%), jpeg 85,500 → 86,782 (+1.50%), ibex 57,700 → 57,758 (+0.10%), uart 41,800 → 40,253 (−3.70%) and fft 84,700 → 82,921 (−2.10%), four designs are flagged: all but ibex. The band should sit above the engine's seed noise; if reruns of the baseline already vary by 0.8%, a 0.5% band flags noise. That is why deterministic engines matter: with bit-identical reruns the band can be tight, and any movement at all is real. Flagged designs go to the model or the human as feedback, with the per-design numbers.

## Proving only intended designs moved

A differential check asks a sharper question than a gate: did the change affect exactly what it should? A new derate plug-in meant to touch only fft is run on the suite, and WNS is compared with an absolute tolerance of 2 ps. Results: riscv32i −35 → −26, aes −37 → −33, gcd −12 → −10, fft −49 → −30, ibex −2 → −7. fft moved by 19 ps, as intended. Among the others, riscv32i (9 ps), aes (4 ps) and ibex (5 ps) exceed 2 ps, while gcd (2 ps) does not. Three unintended movers mean the plug-in's condition fires more broadly than claimed, so the change is rejected or its rule narrowed. The same idea applies at finer grain: compare per-path slacks and require that only paths through the targeted cells changed.

## Going deeper

The agent-first notes in this curriculum on golden and differential testing; the metrics and regression scripts of OpenROAD-flow-scripts.

label: Sandboxed plug-in builds
prereqs: Distributed runs, containers and the cloud
lesson:
# Sandboxed plug-in builds

In an agent harness, model-written plug-in code is compiled and run many times an hour. That code is untrusted, the designs it touches are confidential, and the loop must be fast and reproducible. A sandboxed build answers all three: isolated builds with resource limits and no network, modular builds with a compiler cache, and pinned offline toolchains, so every iteration is safe, quick and repeatable.

## The sandbox around a plug-in build

The harness builds and runs each candidate plug-in inside a sandbox: a container or similar isolated environment with no outbound network, so code cannot exfiltrate design data or pull in unreviewed dependencies, and with limits on CPU, memory and wall-clock time, enforced on Linux by mechanisms such as control groups. An infinite loop becomes a time-limit failure and a runaway allocation becomes a memory-limit failure, both reported back to the model instead of harming the host. The core is visible only as read-only headers and prebuilt libraries, so a plug-in edit cannot silently turn into a core edit. The build is modular: the plug-in compiles as its own unit against the stable interface, so an edit rebuilds only the plug-in, not the engine.

## Iteration time with a compiler cache

A compiler cache such as ccache returns stored object files when a unit's preprocessed input and flags are unchanged. With $U$ units, hit rate $h$, hit cost $t_h$, miss cost $t_m$, link time $L$ and test time $T$, one iteration takes $U(h t_h + (1-h) t_m) + L + T$. Example: $U = 20$, $h = 0.85$, $t_h = 0.2$ s, $t_m = 12$ s, $L = 6$ s, $T = 30$ s gives $20(0.17 + 1.8) + 36 = 75.4$ s, so $\lfloor 3600/75.4 \rfloor = 47$ iterations per hour. A cold build costs $20 \times 12 + 36 = 276$ s, so the cache gives a speedup of $276/75.4 = 3.66$. The fixed link and test time caps the gain; past a point, faster golden tests matter more than a better hit rate. The hit rate itself depends on the build's structure: a plug-in that includes a header the core changes often will miss on every unit after each core update, while a plug-in that sees only a small, stable interface header keeps hitting. Narrow interfaces therefore speed up the agent loop as well as making it safer, and modular builds keep the number of units an edit touches small.

## Pinned offline toolchains

A build that fetches the latest compiler can pass on Monday and fail on Tuesday with no code change. The sandbox therefore uses a pinned toolchain: exact compiler, library and build-tool versions, often in a container image referenced by an immutable content digest rather than a moving tag such as latest. Dependency sources come from a local mirror, so builds stay offline and unchanged even if an upstream project disappears. Reproducible builds go one step further: identical source and toolchain should give bit-identical binaries, which requires stripping embedded timestamps and normalizing absolute paths. A promoted skill records the toolchain digest and flags that built it, so the same binary can be rebuilt and audited later, and a regression can be traced to a code change rather than an environment change.

## Going deeper

The agent-first notes in this curriculum on the harness loop and sandboxing; the ccache documentation; the Reproducible Builds project documentation.

problems.e: If a plug-in edit triggered a full core rebuild, the loop would take minutes per try.

label: Deterministic, seedable engines
lesson:
# Deterministic, seedable engines

An engine is deterministic when the same inputs, parameters and seed always give the same result, whatever the thread count or machine. For a human user this is convenience. For an agent it is a prerequisite: differential tests, debugging by replay and tool-grounded rewards all assume that a difference in output was caused by a difference in input. This concept covers how to build such engines and what to record with their results.

## Same seed, same result

Every random choice should come from a generator created from an explicit seed and passed to the code that needs it, never from the time of day or a global generator that threads consume in arrival order. Tie-breaking must use stable keys: comparing pointer addresses gives different answers on each run because allocation addresses change. Iterating a hash map to decide an order is another trap, since iteration order can vary; sort by a stable key first. For parallel code, fix the partition of work and the order in which partial results are merged, so that 8 threads and 16 threads produce the same floating-point sums. A placer run with seed 7 that reports a different HPWL on 8 and 16 threads has failed this property, even though each run on its own looks fine.

## Recording what a result depends on

A result is reproducible only if everything it depends on is recorded. A result manifest stores the engine version and build, every parameter, the seed, the thread count and content hashes of every input file. Hashes matter because a path can point to a file that was edited after the run; the hash identifies the exact bytes. When a flow runs five seeds and keeps the best, the manifest must store the chosen run's seed, not just the list. If two results differ while their manifests are identical, the engine has a hidden source of nondeterminism, something it depends on but does not record, and that is a bug to find, not noise to accept.

## Why agents need determinism

A differential test compares a baseline and a candidate. If baseline reruns already differ, the comparison cannot attribute any difference to the change. An RL reward computed by running a nondeterministic engine on a model's output is noisy, so the model learns more slowly and may be rewarded for luck. A failure that vanishes on rerun cannot be bisected or fixed. Determinism does not remove seed sensitivity: a placer may legitimately give different QoR for different seeds. When it does, an agent comparing two parameter settings should run several seeds per setting and compare distributions, not single runs; determinism guarantees that each of those runs is itself reproducible.

## Going deeper

The agent-first notes in this curriculum on determinism and testing; literature on deterministic parallel placement and routing in OpenROAD and elsewhere.

problems.q:
An engine iterates a hash map of nets to decide routing order. Results vary between runs. What fix keeps the speed and restores determinism?

A) Sort the nets by a stable key before ordering them

B) Add more threads

C) Seed the hash with the clock

D) Use a larger hash table
problems.a: Sort the nets by a stable key before ordering them
problems.e: Hash iteration order can vary; a stable sort makes the order a function of the data.

problems.q:
A router breaks ties between equal-cost paths by comparing pointer addresses. Why is that a problem?

A) Addresses change between runs, so ties resolve differently

B) Ties never occur in routing

C) It makes the router slower

D) Pointers are always equal
problems.a: Addresses change between runs, so ties resolve differently
problems.e: Tie-breaking must use stable keys such as object ids, not memory addresses.

problems.q:
A placer run with seed 7 on 8 threads gives a different HPWL than seed 7 on 16 threads. What determinism property fails?

A) Results must be faster with more threads

B) Results must not depend on the thread count

C) Results must be identical across designs

D) Results must not depend on the seed
problems.a: Results must not depend on the thread count
problems.e: A deterministic parallel engine fixes partitions and merge order so the thread count changes speed, not results.

problems.q:
Why hash the input design files in the manifest instead of storing only their paths?

A) Hashes are shorter to type

B) Hashes speed up the engine

C) Paths are illegal in manifests

D) A path can point to changed content; a hash identifies the exact bytes
problems.a: A path can point to changed content; a hash identifies the exact bytes
problems.e: Content hashes catch silent edits to inputs.

problems.q:
Why hash the input design files in the manifest instead of storing only their paths?

A) Hashes are shorter to type

B) Hashes speed up the engine

C) Paths are illegal in manifests

D) A path can point to changed content; a hash identifies the exact bytes
problems.a: A path can point to changed content; a hash identifies the exact bytes
problems.e: Content hashes catch silent edits to inputs.

problems.q:
A flow runs placement with five seeds and keeps the best. What must the manifest store for the chosen result?

A) Nothing, since the best is obvious

B) The seed of the chosen run, not just the seed list

C) The worst seed

D) Only the number of seeds
problems.a: The seed of the chosen run, not just the seed list
problems.e: To reproduce the chosen result you need its exact seed.

problems.q:
An agent compares two parameter sets with one run each on a seed-sensitive engine. What should it do instead?

A) Disable the seed

B) Use a single seed, chosen at random

C) Run several seeds per setting and compare distributions

D) Compare only the first iteration
problems.a: Run several seeds per setting and compare distributions
problems.e: When results vary by seed, one run per setting cannot separate the parameter effect from seed noise.

problems.q:
An RL reward comes from running a placer on the model's output. The placer is nondeterministic. What happens to learning?

A) The reward is noisy, so the model learns slower and may chase luck

B) Learning becomes faster

C) Nothing changes

D) The reward becomes exact
problems.a: The reward is noisy, so the model learns slower and may chase luck
problems.e: Noise in a tool-grounded reward blurs which actions were actually better.

problems.q:
An RL reward comes from running a placer on the model's output. The placer is nondeterministic. What happens to learning?

A) Nothing changes

B) The reward becomes exact

C) The reward is noisy, so the model learns slower and may chase luck

D) Learning becomes faster
problems.a: The reward is noisy, so the model learns slower and may chase luck
problems.e: Noise in a tool-grounded reward blurs which actions were actually better.

label: MCP tool wrappers around OpenROAD
prereqs: Engines as agent tools over MCP
lesson:
# MCP tool wrappers around OpenROAD

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets an engine be exposed as a set of typed tools that any agent can discover and call. Wrapping OpenROAD this way turns its Tcl commands into a contract: named tools with input and output schemas, structured results, sessions that hold a design, and a sandbox around the process. Designing that wrapper well is a small exercise in API design with large consequences for every agent that uses it.

## Typed tools over an engine

An MCP server advertises tools, each with a name, a plain-language description and a JSON schema for its inputs and outputs. For OpenROAD, a tool such as report_timing might take a path group and a count and return structured fields: WNS, TNS and a list of worst paths with their slacks and endpoints, rather than the raw log text. Input schemas validate before the engine runs: a utilization declared as a number between 0.1 and 0.9 rejects 45 (a percent typed as a fraction) with a clear error instead of an absurd floorplan. The description states preconditions, such as "requires a placed design", because the agent reads descriptions to decide which tool to call and in which order, exactly as it reads skill manifests.

## Choosing tool granularity

Granularity decides how usable the server is. A single eval_tcl tool that runs any string is powerful but has no typed contract, no validation, unstructured output and no way to audit or restrict what runs. The opposite extreme, one tool per database accessor, floods the agent with round trips. Coarse actions work best: initialize the floorplan, run global placement with these parameters, repair timing, report timing. Per-object operations should be batched, so moving 10,000 cells is one call with a list, not 10,000 calls, the same reason a plug-in is called per batch rather than per cell. Long operations such as detailed routing, which can take an hour, should start a job and return an id, with a separate tool to poll or cancel it.

## Sessions, sandboxing and structured results

Loading a large ODB is expensive, so the server keeps a session holding the current design between calls, and each tool acts on that state. When the design is customer IP, the OpenROAD process and its data stay on-site, in a sandbox with resource limits and no outbound network; only structured results cross to the agent. Tools should be idempotent where possible: calling set_place_density twice with the same value leaves the same state, so an agent that retries after a timeout does no harm. Every call is logged with its arguments, the engine version and a checksum of the resulting database, so a session can be audited, replayed from scratch and reverted, which keeps agent actions reviewable in the same way a code change is.

## Going deeper

The Model Context Protocol specification; the OpenROAD Tcl and Python API documentation; the agent-first notes in this curriculum on engines as agent tools.

problems.q:
Why should an MCP tool's description state its preconditions, such as requiring a placed design?

A) Preconditions are enforced by MCP itself

B) The agent reads descriptions to choose and order tool calls

C) Descriptions are compiled into the engine

D) It hides the tool from agents
problems.a: The agent reads descriptions to choose and order tool calls
problems.e: Like a skill manifest, a description is how the caller decides what to call.

problems.q:
A tool's input schema declares utilization as a number between 0.1 and 0.9. What does that buy?

A) The engine runs twice as fast

B) The agent never needs to read results

C) Bad arguments are rejected before the engine runs

D) The DB is saved automatically
problems.a: Bad arguments are rejected before the engine runs
problems.e: Validation at the boundary turns a malformed call into an immediate, clear error.

problems.q:
An MCP tool report_timing returns its result. Which form is most useful to an agent?

A) Nothing; it only prints to stdout

B) A screenshot of the GUI

C) Structured fields such as WNS, TNS and a list of worst paths

D) The raw log with color codes
problems.a: Structured fields such as WNS, TNS and a list of worst paths
problems.e: Structured output can be parsed and compared reliably.

problems.q:
A tool run_detailed_route can take an hour. How should its interface handle that?

A) Start a job and return an id, with a separate tool to poll status

B) Split it into one call per net

C) Block silently for an hour

D) Return a fake result immediately
problems.a: Start a job and return an id, with a separate tool to poll status
problems.e: Long jobs need asynchronous handling so the agent can wait, poll or cancel.

problems.q:
A tool run_detailed_route can take an hour. How should its interface handle that?

A) Split it into one call per net

B) Start a job and return an id, with a separate tool to poll status

C) Block silently for an hour

D) Return a fake result immediately
problems.a: Start a job and return an id, with a separate tool to poll status
problems.e: Long jobs need asynchronous handling so the agent can wait, poll or cancel.

problems.q:
A tool run_detailed_route can take an hour. How should its interface handle that?

A) Split it into one call per net

B) Block silently for an hour

C) Return a fake result immediately

D) Start a job and return an id, with a separate tool to poll status
problems.a: Start a job and return an id, with a separate tool to poll status
problems.e: Long jobs need asynchronous handling so the agent can wait, poll or cancel.

problems.q:
Where should the OpenROAD process behind an MCP server run when the design is customer IP?

A) On-site, in a sandbox with limits and no outbound network

B) On any public server

C) Inside the model provider's cloud by default

D) In the agent's chat window
problems.a: On-site, in a sandbox with limits and no outbound network
problems.e: The IP boundary is part of the architecture: engines and data stay on-site.

problems.q:
An agent calls set_place_density twice with the same value. Why should the tool be idempotent?

A) Idempotent tools run faster

B) The second call must undo the first

C) Retries then leave the design in the same state

D) Agents never retry
problems.a: Retries then leave the design in the same state
problems.e: Agents retry after timeouts; idempotent tools make retries safe.

problems.q:
Where should the OpenROAD process behind an MCP server run when the design is customer IP?

A) Inside the model provider's cloud by default

B) On-site, in a sandbox with limits and no outbound network

C) In the agent's chat window

D) On any public server
problems.a: On-site, in a sandbox with limits and no outbound network
problems.e: The IP boundary is part of the architecture: engines and data stay on-site.
